quiz.q: In the Indian view of self, the boundary between self and others is:
quiz.explain: The Indian view sees the self as able to include family and community; the Western view sees a firmer boundary.
steps: In the Indian view, the self can expand to include family and community.
So the boundary between self and others is flexible.
The Western view sees it as relatively fixed.
Answer: Flexible, expanding to include others
quiz.mistake: Applies the Western fixed-boundary view to India.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Many Asian cultures, including India, are described as collectivistic.

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

topics.title: Personality: meaning and early type approaches

learn.hook: Roman actors wore masks called 'persona' to show their roles. Our word 'personality' comes from that mask — but personality is far more than what shows on the surface.
points: Personality comes from the Latin word 'persona', the mask used by actors in Roman theatre. It refers to our characteristic ways of responding to individuals and situations.

Characteristics: it has both physical and psychological components; its main features are relatively stable across time and consistent across situations; yet it is dynamic, changing in response to internal or external demands.
Studying personality helps us understand and predict behaviour and helps in guidance, selection and therapy.
Type approaches group people into types. Hippocrates proposed four types based on bodily fluids (humours): sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic.

Charak Samhita (Ayurveda) classifies people by three humoral elements, the tridosha: vata, pitta and kapha. The theory of trigunas describes sattva (cleanliness, truthfulness, discipline, detachment), rajas (intense activity, desire for sense gratification, envy, materialism) and tamas (anger, arrogance, laziness, helplessness); all three are present in everyone in different degrees.

example.q: A person is described as disciplined, truthful and detached from material gains. Which guna is dominant?
steps: Sattva includes cleanliness, truthfulness, dutifulness, detachment and discipline.
Rajas involves intense activity and desire; tamas involves anger and laziness.
So the description fits sattva.
example.answer: Sattva.

learn.reallife: The Ayurveda ideas of vata, pitta and kapha still appear in Indian wellness talk today — they are one of the oldest type approaches to personality.

steps: Hippocrates proposed four types based on bodily fluids (humours).

Answer: Bodily fluids (humours)
quiz.mistake: Confuses with Sheldon's body types.

quiz.q: The tridosha of Charak Samhita refers to:
quiz.explain: Charak Samhita classifies people by vata, pitta and kapha.
steps: Charak Samhita's tridosha = vata, pitta and kapha.

Answer: Vata, pitta and kapha
quiz.mistake: Mixes the tridosha with the trigunas.

steps: Envy, intense activity and desire for material things.

Answer: Rajas
quiz.mistake: Thinks envy and anger belong only to tamas.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): According to the triguna theory, every person has some sattva, rajas and tamas.
Reason (R): The tridosha of Charak Samhita consists of vata, pitta and kapha.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the tridosha is a different classification and does not explain the presence of the three gunas in everyone.
steps: A: everyone has some sattva, rajas and tamas – true.
R: tridosha consists of vata, pitta and kapha – true.
The tridosha is a separate classification and does not explain the gunas.
So both are true, but R is not the correct explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the trigunas and the tridosha.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of Hippocrates' four types?
quiz.explain: Hippocrates' types are sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic.
steps: Hippocrates' four: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic.
Ectomorph is Sheldon; pitta is Charak; extravert is Jung.
Answer: Phlegmatic
quiz.mistake: Mixes typologies from different theorists.

quiz.q: Why do psychologists study personality?

To fix one label on a person forever
quiz.explain: Personality helps explain and predict behaviour and supports guidance and selection.
steps: Studying personality helps understand and predict behaviour across situations.

Answer: To understand and predict how people are likely to behave across situations
quiz.mistake: Thinks personality study only labels or diagnoses.

revise.summary: Personality, from the Latin 'persona' (mask), is our characteristic way of responding to people and situations: stable yet dynamic. Early type approaches include Hippocrates' four humours, Charak Samhita's tridosha and the trigunas.

Tridosha: vata, pitta, kapha

topics.title: Body types, introverts–extraverts and Type A/B/C/D

learn.hook: Always rushing, impatient in a queue, checking the time every minute? Researchers found such 'Type A' behaviour linked with heart disease.
points: William Sheldon linked body build with temperament: endomorph (fat, soft, round — relaxed and sociable), mesomorph (strong, muscular, rectangular — energetic and courageous) and ectomorph (thin, long, fragile — brainy, artistic and introverted). Body-build types are poor predictors of behaviour.
Carl Jung grouped people into introverts (prefer to be alone, shy, withdraw under stress) and extraverts (sociable, outgoing, seek people when stressed).

Friedman and Rosenman described Type-A personality: high motivation, impatience, feeling short of time, always in a hurry, burdened with work. Type-A people are more prone to hypertension and coronary heart disease (CHD). Type-B is the absence of Type-A traits.
Morris suggested Type-C (cooperative, unassertive, patient, suppress negative emotions such as anger, comply with authority; prone to cancer) and Type-D (prone to depression).
Type approaches are simple and easy to use, but people rarely fit neatly into a single type; behaviour is more complex and variable.

example.q: Vikram eats lunch while answering emails, honks repeatedly in traffic and feels he never has enough time. Which type is he, and what health risk is linked to it?
steps: Impatience, hurry and time pressure are Type-A features (Friedman and Rosenman).
Type-A is associated with hypertension and coronary heart disease.
example.answer: Type-A; higher risk of hypertension and coronary heart disease.

learn.reallife: Mumbai's corporate workers racing for the 8:12 local while answering calls are textbook Type-A behaviour — doctors in metros increasingly see stress-linked heart problems in young adults.

topics.title: Trait theories: Allport, Cattell, Eysenck and the Big Five

learn.hook: Describe your best friend in five words. Chances are your words map onto just five big dimensions that psychologists found across cultures, including India.
points: Traits are relatively enduring attributes on which people differ (such as honesty or sociability). Unlike types, traits are dimensions on which everyone can be placed.

Gordon Allport: cardinal traits (highly generalised; the goal around which a whole life revolves, e.g. Mahatma Gandhi's non-violence), central traits (less pervasive but common, e.g. honest, punctual) and secondary traits (least generalised, e.g. 'likes mangoes').

Raymond Cattell used factor analysis to find source traits (stable building blocks of personality) and surface traits (resulting from interactions of source traits). His 16 Personality Factor Questionnaire (16 PF) is widely used.

Hans Eysenck: two broad, biologically based dimensions — neuroticism vs emotional stability, and extraversion vs introversion; later a third, psychoticism vs sociability. Measured by the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ).
Five-Factor Model (Paul Costa and Robert McCrae): openness to experience, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism and conscientiousness (OCEAN). It has been found across cultures, including India.

example.q: Riya is curious, plans her work carefully, is talkative, kind to everyone, and stays calm under pressure. Rate her on the Big Five.
steps: Curious → high openness.
Plans carefully → high conscientiousness.
Talkative → high extraversion.
Kind → high agreeableness.
Calm under pressure → low neuroticism.
example.answer: High O, C, E and A; low N.

learn.reallife: Some Indian companies use personality questionnaires like the 16 PF or Big Five-based tools when hiring, for example looking for conscientiousness in roles such as auditing.

topics.title: Freud: levels of consciousness and structure of personality

learn.hook: You call your teacher 'Mummy' by mistake and the class giggles. Freud would say your unconscious just slipped out!
points: Sigmund Freud described three levels of consciousness: conscious (thoughts and feelings we are currently aware of), preconscious (material we can become aware of if we attend to it) and unconscious (thoughts and desires we are unaware of, including instinctive drives and unacceptable wishes). He used free association and dream analysis to study the unconscious.
Id: the source of instinctual energy, seeking immediate gratification of primitive needs, sexual desires and aggressive impulses; it works on the pleasure principle and ignores morality and reality.
Ego: grows out of the id and satisfies its needs in socially appropriate ways; it works on the reality principle and is often called the executive of personality.
Superego: the moral branch, the internalised values and standards (often from parents); it works on the moral principle and judges whether gratification is right or wrong.
Libido is the instinctual life force that energises the id (linked to Eros, the life instinct). Freud later also proposed Thanatos, the death instinct.

example.q: Ravi sees an unattended expensive pen. One part of him wants to grab it, another says 'Someone may see you', and a third says 'Stealing is wrong'. Identify each.
steps: Wanting it immediately = id (pleasure principle).
Thinking about real consequences = ego (reality principle).
Judging it morally wrong = superego (moral principle).
example.answer: Id: 'grab it'; Ego: 'someone may see'; Superego: 'stealing is wrong'.

learn.reallife: In a group chat argument, the id wants to send an angry reply, the superego says 'Be respectful', and the ego drafts a calm message — Freud's three systems at work on WhatsApp.

topics.title: Defence mechanisms and psychosexual stages

learn.hook: Failed a test? 'The paper was unfair anyway!' That convenient excuse might be your ego defending itself.
points: When the ego cannot balance id, superego and reality, anxiety results. Defence mechanisms reduce anxiety by distorting reality. Everyone uses them sometimes; relying heavily on them is unhealthy.

Repression (the most common): anxiety-provoking thoughts are pushed into the unconscious. Projection: attributing one's own unacceptable traits to others. Denial: totally refusing to accept reality. Reaction formation: behaving opposite to one's true feelings. Rationalisation: giving a reasonable-sounding excuse for unreasonable feelings or behaviour.

Psychosexual stages: oral (first year; pleasure through the mouth), anal (about 2–3 years; toilet training), phallic (about 4–5 years; Oedipus complex in boys, Electra complex in girls, resolved by identifying with the same-sex parent), latency (about 7 years to puberty; urges are dormant, energy goes into social and school activities), genital (adolescence onwards; mature sexuality).

Fixation: getting stuck at an earlier stage because its conflict was not resolved. Regression: going back to an earlier stage's behaviour under stress (for example, an older child starting thumb-sucking when a new sibling arrives).

example.q: Sumit, who strongly dislikes his new classmate, is extremely sweet and overly praising towards him. Which defence mechanism is this?
steps: His true feeling is dislike.
His behaviour is the opposite — exaggerated friendliness.
Behaving opposite to true feelings = reaction formation.
example.answer: Reaction formation.

learn.reallife: After a big loss, a team captain saying 'The pitch suited them, we weren't even trying hard' may be rationalising — it protects self-esteem but blocks learning.

topics.title: Post-Freudian approaches and criticisms

learn.hook: Freud's students didn't just copy him — they argued with him. Their disagreements gave us ideas like the inferiority complex and the identity crisis.
points: Carl Jung — analytical psychology: personality has competing forces within the individual. Besides the personal unconscious, there is a collective unconscious shared by all humanity, containing archetypes (primordial images, such as the mother or the hero, seen in myths and dreams).

Karen Horney stressed social and cultural factors. Parental indifference, discouragement and erratic behaviour can make a child feel insecure — basic anxiety — and resentful (basic hostility). She also challenged Freud's view of women.

Alfred Adler — individual psychology: behaviour is purposeful and goal-directed. Feelings of inadequacy create an inferiority complex; striving for superiority to overcome it drives personality development.

Erich Fromm saw humans as basically social beings; qualities such as the desire for freedom, justice and truth develop through relationships with others. Erik Erikson stressed rational, conscious ego processes and psychosocial development, including the identity crisis of adolescence.

Criticisms of psychodynamic theories: based mainly on case studies without a strong scientific base; small, unusual samples; concepts that are hard to define and test; and Freud's use of males as the prototype, neglecting women.

example.q: A 16-year-old keeps asking, 'Who am I? What do I want to become?' and tries out new interests and styles. Which theorist's idea fits best?
steps: The question is about forming a sense of identity in adolescence.
Erikson described the identity crisis as a key task of adolescence.
example.answer: Erik Erikson's identity crisis.

learn.reallife: Similar hero stories — a brave hero, a wise mentor, a final battle — appear in the Ramayana, Greek myths and modern films. Jung would point to archetypes from the collective unconscious.

topics.title: Behavioural, cultural and humanistic approaches

learn.hook: Is your personality what you learned, what your community's way of life demanded, or the person you're striving to become? Three approaches give three answers.
points: Behavioural approach: personality is the person's learned responses to the environment. Its core elements are stimulus, response and reinforcement (for example, hunger is the stimulus, eating the response, satisfaction the reinforcement). Classical conditioning (Pavlov), operant conditioning (Skinner) and observational learning (Bandura) all shape personality.
Cultural approach: personality traits are adaptations to the ecology and culture of a group. A group's economic maintenance system — how it earns its living — shapes valued traits.

In hunting-gathering, nomadic communities (for example, the Birhor of Jharkhand's forest regions), skills like independence, autonomy and achievement are valued; in settled agricultural societies, obedience, nurturance and responsibility are emphasised.

Humanistic approach — Carl Rogers: the fully functioning person; the self-concept; real self (what we are) vs ideal self (what we would like to be). A small gap brings happiness; a large gap brings dissatisfaction. Unconditional positive regard helps build a healthy self-concept.

Abraham Maslow: self-actualisation is the state of reaching one's fullest potential. Self-actualised, healthy people accept themselves and others, are realistic, creative, autonomous and capable of deep relationships and peak experiences.

example.q: Kavya dreams of being a confident public speaker (ideal self) but sees herself as shy and hesitant (real self). According to Rogers, what will she feel, and what helps?
steps: Real self (shy) is far from ideal self (confident speaker).
A large real–ideal gap leads to dissatisfaction and unhappiness.
Unconditional positive regard from others helps her accept herself and close the gap.
example.answer: She will feel dissatisfied; unconditional positive regard and acceptance help.

learn.reallife: When a coach praises a young player only when she wins, love feels conditional. Rogers argued that accepting the person regardless of results builds healthier self-esteem — something good Indian sports academies now try.

topics.title: Assessing personality: self-report measures

learn.hook: Question: 'I always tell the truth.' Tick yes or no. Would everyone answer honestly? That's the central problem of self-report tests.
points: Personality assessment helps understand and predict behaviour with minimum error, for purposes such as diagnosis, training, placement and counselling.

Self-report measures are fairly structured tests where people answer about themselves, often on rating scales. The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI), developed by Hathaway and McKinley to aid psychiatric diagnosis, is widely used; MMPI-2 has 567 statements and 10 subscales. In India, Mallick and Joshi developed the Jodhpur Multiphasic Personality Inventory (JMPI) along MMPI lines.

The Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ) assesses dimensions such as extraversion–introversion, emotional stability–neuroticism and psychoticism. Cattell's 16 PF measures 16 personality factors and is used with high school students, college students and adults; Indian versions exist.
Problems: social desirability — answering in a socially acceptable way rather than truthfully; acquiescence — tendency to agree ('yes') with items regardless of their content.

example.q: A student answers 'yes' to almost every item, even to contradictory items such as 'I enjoy parties' and 'I avoid parties'. Which problem is this?
steps: Agreeing with items regardless of content = acquiescence.
Contradictory 'yes' answers show the response is not based on the item's meaning.
example.answer: Acquiescence.

learn.reallife: In job applications, candidates may tick 'I never lose my temper' to look good. Recruiters using personality questionnaires watch out for this social desirability bias.

topics.title: Projective techniques

learn.hook: Look at a cloud. One friend sees a dragon, another a dancing girl. Projective tests use exactly this: ambiguous pictures to reveal hidden feelings.
points: Projective techniques are based on psychoanalytic theory: when given an ambiguous or unstructured stimulus, a person projects unconscious feelings, desires and needs onto it. Responses are interpreted by trained experts; scoring is complex and less objective.

Rorschach Inkblot Test (Hermann Rorschach): 10 symmetrical inkblots — five black and white, two with some red, three in pastel colours. Two phases: performance proper (the person says what they see) and inquiry (a detailed report of the responses).
Thematic Apperception Test (TAT; Morgan and Murray, 1935): 30 black-and-white picture cards and one blank card; the person makes up stories. Uma Chaudhury developed an Indian adaptation.
Rosenzweig's Picture-Frustration Study (P-F Study) uses cartoon-like pictures of frustrating situations to assess how people express aggression; Pareek adapted it for India.

Sentence Completion Test: incomplete sentences (e.g., 'My father...') reveal attitudes, motives and conflicts. Draw-a-Person Test: the person draws a person, then one of the opposite sex, and makes up a story about them.

example.q: A psychologist shows Neel a card with a blurry picture of a boy sitting near a broken violin and asks him to tell a story about what led up to it and how it ends. Which test is this?
steps: Picture cards + making up a story about what happened, what is happening and what will happen.
This is the method of the Thematic Apperception Test.
example.answer: Thematic Apperception Test (TAT).

learn.reallife: Clinical psychologists at institutes like NIMHANS may use projective tests alongside interviews, never alone, because scoring them requires extensive training.

topics.title: Behavioural analysis: interviews, ratings, nominations and situational tests

learn.hook: A teacher rates a student 'excellent' in every trait just because she is great at cricket. That single bright spot is colouring everything — psychologists call it the halo effect.
points: Behavioural analysis uses a person's behaviour in real situations to assess personality.

Interview: structured (specific questions in a set order) or unstructured (flexible questions guided by the person's responses). Observation by trained observers gives rich data but is time-consuming and can be influenced by the observer.

Behavioural ratings: raters (teachers, peers, supervisors) place people into categories or rate them on traits. Errors: halo effect (a single favourable or unfavourable trait colours all ratings), middle category bias (rating everyone in the middle, avoiding extremes) and extreme response bias (rating at the extreme ends).
Nominations: peers who know a person well nominate people with certain qualities; useful and fairly reliable, though personal biases can creep in.
Situational tests: the person is observed in a created situation; the most common is the situational stress test, where tasks are done with others who have been instructed to be non-cooperative.

example.q: An interviewer rates a well-dressed candidate highly on honesty, intelligence and teamwork without evidence. Which error occurred?
steps: One favourable feature (appearance) influenced ratings on unrelated traits.
That is the halo effect.
example.answer: Halo effect.

learn.reallife: Services Selection Boards (SSB) that pick officers for the Indian Armed Forces use group tasks and situational tests, observing how candidates act under pressure, along with interviews.

topics.title: What is stress? Eustress, distress and cognitive appraisal

learn.hook: Two students get the same board timetable. One says 'Finally, a chance to show what I've got!' The other says 'I'm doomed.' Same event — very different stress. Why?
points: Life brings challenges; how we adjust to them affects our well-being. Stress is the pattern of responses an organism makes to a stimulus event that disturbs its equilibrium and exceeds its ability to cope. The event causing it is a stressor.
The word stress comes from the Latin 'strictus', meaning tight or narrow (and the verb 'stringere', to tighten).
Hans Selye used 'eustress' for a healthy, positive level of stress that motivates and improves performance; 'distress' is excessive, harmful stress.

Richard Lazarus's cognitive theory: primary appraisal judges a new or changing event as positive, neutral or negative; negative events are judged for harm (damage already done), threat (possible future damage) or challenge (confidence of overcoming it, with possible positive outcomes).

Secondary appraisal is the assessment of one's coping abilities and resources — whether they will be enough to deal with the harm, threat or challenge. Stress is felt when demands seem to exceed resources.

example.q: Ayesha learns that her science practical exam is next week. She thinks 'This could go badly' (1), then 'But I've practised every experiment and my teacher will help' (2). Label the two appraisals and predict her stress.
steps: (1) Judging the event as possibly harmful in the future = primary appraisal of threat.
(2) Evaluating her preparation and teacher's support = secondary appraisal of coping resources.
Resources seem adequate, so stress is likely to be manageable — even eustress.
example.answer: (1) Primary appraisal (threat); (2) Secondary appraisal; moderate, manageable stress.

learn.reallife: Before a World Cup final, a fast bowler may feel the pressure as a challenge rather than a threat. Sports psychologists working with Indian teams train players to re-appraise pressure exactly this way.

topics.title: Signs, symptoms and types of stress

learn.hook: Headache, snapping at your sibling, and staring at the same page for 20 minutes — three different signs, one possible cause: stress.
points: Signs and symptoms of stress can be physical (headaches, fatigue, sleep problems), emotional (irritability, anxiety, mood swings) and behavioural (changes in eating, withdrawal, poor work). Each person shows stress in their own way.

Physical and environmental stress: physical demands change the body's state (overexertion, poor nutrition, injury, lack of sleep); environmental stressors are unavoidable aspects of surroundings (air pollution, crowding, noise, summer heat, winter cold) and disasters (floods, earthquakes, fire).

Psychological stress comes from within: frustration (blocking of needs and motives), conflicts (between two or more incompatible needs or motives), internal pressures (beliefs like 'I must do everything perfectly') and social pressures (people making excessive demands on us).

Social stress is induced by interaction with other people — death or illness in the family, strained relationships, trouble with neighbours. Even a party can be stressful for someone who prefers solitude.

example.q: Classify: (a) Delhi's winter smog, (b) wanting to join both the dance club and the coding club that meet at the same time, (c) a quarrel with a close friend.
steps: (a) Unavoidable surroundings = environmental stress.
(b) Two incompatible motives = conflict, a psychological stress.
(c) Arises from interaction with others = social stress.
example.answer: (a) Environmental, (b) Psychological (conflict), (c) Social.

learn.reallife: Mumbai's packed local trains, Chennai's summer heat and Assam's annual floods are everyday reminders of environmental stress for millions of Indians.

topics.title: Sources of stress: life events, hassles and traumatic events

learn.hook: Getting married, changing city, a new job — happy events! Yet each one can raise your stress score on a famous scale.
points: Life events: major or minor, sudden or gradual changes such as moving house, a new job, marriage or loss of a loved one. Holmes and Rahe's Social Readjustment Rating Scale (SRRS) gives each event a value based on how much readjustment it needs; death of a spouse ranks highest.
Both pleasant and unpleasant events require readjustment and add to stress; a high total score within a short period is linked with a higher risk of illness.

Hassles: everyday irritations of daily life — noisy surroundings, commuting, water or power cuts, traffic jams, quarrelsome neighbours. The more hassles people report, the lower their psychological well-being tends to be.
Traumatic events: extreme events such as fire, train or road accidents, robbery, earthquakes or tsunamis. Their effects can last a long time as anxiety, flashbacks, nightmares and intrusive thoughts.

example.q: In one month, Prakash shifts to Hyderabad for a new job, gets married, and deals with daily traffic jams. Which sources of stress are present?
steps: Shifting city, new job and marriage = life events (all need readjustment, even happy ones).
Daily traffic jams = hassles.
example.answer: Life events (relocation, new job, marriage) and hassles (traffic).

learn.reallife: Bengaluru's notorious traffic, daily power cuts in some towns and long ration queues are classic hassles; the 2004 tsunami and the Kedarnath floods of 2013 were traumatic events whose effects lasted years.

topics.title: Effects of stress on mind, body and behaviour

learn.hook: During exam week you forget a formula you knew perfectly, sleep badly and crave junk food. Stress touches emotions, body, thinking and behaviour all at once.
points: Emotional effects: mood swings, erratic behaviour, anxiety, depression, feelings of alienation, and physical and mental tension.

Physiological effects: the adrenal glands release stress hormones such as epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and also cortisol. Effects include faster heart rate, expansion of air passages, constriction of blood vessels and slowing of digestion.

Cognitive effects: poor concentration and reduced short-term memory capacity. Behavioural effects: disrupted sleep, disturbed eating, more caffeine or other stimulants, increased absenteeism and reduced work performance.
Burnout is a state of physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion that follows prolonged, high stress.
Chronic stress is linked with illnesses such as coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, ulcers and asthma, as well as lowered immunity.

example.q: A software engineer has worked 80-hour weeks for a year. He now feels drained, cynical about work and physically tired all the time. What is this state called?
steps: Prolonged, intense stress at work.
Physical, emotional and psychological exhaustion together.
This is burnout.
example.answer: Burnout.

learn.reallife: Doctors and nurses during the COVID-19 waves in India reported high levels of burnout — long shifts and constant pressure exhausted body and mind. If stress ever feels overwhelming, Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free, confidential support.

topics.title: General Adaptation Syndrome (Selye)

learn.hook: First the panic, then the long grind, then the crash. Hans Selye mapped this three-stage pattern in the body's response to prolonged stress.
points: Hans Selye studied animals exposed to stressors such as high temperature, X-rays and insulin injections, and patients with injuries and illnesses. He found a similar pattern of bodily response, the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS).

Stage 1 — Alarm reaction: the presence of a stressor activates the adrenal–pituitary–cortex system and the sympathetic nervous system; hormones are released and the body's defences are mobilised for 'fight or flight'.
Stage 2 — Resistance: if stress continues, the body tries to cope; the parasympathetic nervous system calls for more careful use of the body's resources.
Stage 3 — Exhaustion: continued exposure to the same or additional stressors drains the body's resources, and stress-related illnesses (such as high blood pressure) become more likely.
Criticism: GAS gives a very limited role to psychological factors such as cognitive appraisal, and people respond differently to the same stressor.

example.q: A farmer faces a long drought. In week 1 he panics (racing heart). For months he works extra hours digging wells. After a year he falls ill. Map these to GAS.
steps: Week 1: sudden mobilisation of the body = alarm reaction.
Months of effort to cope = resistance.
Resources depleted, illness = exhaustion.
example.answer: Alarm → Resistance → Exhaustion.

learn.reallife: Indian Army soldiers posted at Siachen face extreme cold for long periods. Postings there are kept short and rotated; in GAS terms, this limits how long the body must stay in the resistance stage before exhaustion can set in.

topics.title: Stress, the immune system and lifestyle

learn.hook: Ever noticed how many students catch a cold right after board exams? Your mind and your immune system talk to each other.
points: Psychoneuroimmunology studies the links between the mind, the brain (nervous system) and the immune system. Stress can weaken immune functioning.
The immune system guards the body against foreign bodies (antigens) such as viruses. White blood cells (leucocytes) identify and destroy them.

Three kinds of white blood cells: T cells destroy invaders (T-helper cells increase immunological activity and are the cells attacked by HIV); B cells produce antibodies; natural killer cells fight viruses and tumours. Stress can reduce natural killer cell activity.
Stress can push people toward unhealthy lifestyles: poor nutrition, too little sleep and exercise, smoking and alcohol use — which further harm health.
Health-promoting behaviours include a balanced diet, regular exercise, enough sleep, positive thinking and supportive relationships.

example.q: During exam season, Simran sleeps little, survives on chips and gets fever twice. Explain using psychoneuroimmunology and lifestyle.
steps: Exam stress can lower immune activity (for example, natural killer cell activity).
Stress also pushed her into an unhealthy lifestyle: little sleep, poor food.
Both together raise her chances of infection.
example.answer: Stress weakened her immunity directly and indirectly through an unhealthy lifestyle.

learn.reallife: Fit India and Khelo India campaigns encourage daily exercise and balanced diets — health-promoting behaviours that also act as buffers against stress.

topics.title: Coping with stress: strategies and styles

learn.hook: Bad marks in a unit test. Do you (a) make a study plan, (b) cry it out with a friend, or (c) binge-watch a web series and pretend it didn't happen? Each is a coping strategy.
points: Coping is a dynamic, situation-specific reaction to stress — a set of concrete responses aimed at resolving the problem and reducing stress.
Endler and Parker described three strategies. Task-oriented: getting information about the stressful situation and alternatives, setting priorities and acting directly.

Emotion-oriented: efforts to maintain hope and control emotions; venting feelings of anger and frustration; or deciding nothing can be done. Avoidance-oriented: denying or minimising the seriousness of the situation, suppressing stressful thoughts, and replacing them with self-protective thoughts (such as watching TV or calling a friend).

Lazarus and Folkman: problem-focused coping attacks the problem itself (gathering information, changing the situation, altering beliefs), while emotion-focused coping tries to limit emotional disruption with little effort to change the event.
Problem-focused strategies generally work better when the situation can be changed; emotion-focused coping is useful when it cannot (for example, after a loss).

example.q: Classify: (a) Mohit asks his teacher which topics he got wrong and makes a revision plan; (b) Sara tells herself 'it doesn't matter, the test wasn't important' and goes out with friends.
steps: (a) Gathering information and acting on the problem = task-oriented / problem-focused.
(b) Minimising the seriousness and distracting herself = avoidance-oriented.
example.answer: (a) Task-oriented (problem-focused); (b) Avoidance-oriented.

learn.reallife: When a cyclone warning is issued in Odisha, families who stock supplies and move to shelters are using task-oriented coping — and Odisha's preparedness has saved thousands of lives.

topics.title: Stress management techniques

learn.hook: Fighter pilots, surgeons and archers all train their nervous systems. You can too — from slow breathing to watching your own heart rate on a screen.
points: Relaxation techniques reduce symptoms of stress and lower illnesses such as high blood pressure and heart disease. Relaxation often starts with the lower body and moves up to the facial muscles, combined with slow, deep breathing.
Meditation is a yogic method of focusing attention to alter the state of consciousness — concentrating on a mantra, an object or the breath; mindful meditation trains calm awareness.

Biofeedback monitors and reduces the physiological aspects of stress by giving feedback about current physiological activity, often with relaxation training. Three stages: (1) becoming aware of a particular physiological response (e.g. heart rate), (2) learning to control it in quiet conditions, (3) transferring that control to everyday life.
Creative visualisation uses imagery and imagination (e.g. picturing a calm beach); it works best in a quiet, relaxed state with eyes closed and realistic images.

Stress inoculation training (Donald Meichenbaum), a cognitive-behavioural technique, replaces negative, irrational thoughts with positive, rational ones in three phases: assessment, stress reduction techniques, and application and follow-through. Regular exercise (walking, swimming, cycling, skipping) also acts as a stress buffer.

example.q: Put the biofeedback stages in order for a student who gets a racing heart before presentations.
steps: First, she learns to notice her heart rate rising using a monitor.
Next, she practises lowering it in a quiet room using relaxation.
Finally, she uses the same control just before real presentations.
example.answer: Awareness → control in quiet conditions → transfer to everyday life.

learn.reallife: Indian archers and shooters train with breathing and visualisation routines; many schools also start the day with a short meditation or pranayama session.

topics.title: Hardiness and life skills: assertiveness, time management, rational thinking

learn.hook: Some people seem to bounce through tough times. Suzanne Kobasa found they share three Cs — and the good news is these attitudes can be learned.
points: Stress-resistant personality — hardiness (Suzanne Kobasa): a set of beliefs about oneself, the world and how they interact. Its 3 Cs are commitment (to work, family, hobbies and social life), control (a sense of purpose and direction in life) and challenge (seeing changes as normal and positive rather than as threats).
Life skills are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that help us deal effectively with the demands and challenges of daily life.
Assertiveness helps us communicate our feelings, needs, wants and thoughts clearly and confidently — including the ability to say 'no', express opinions without fear and express emotions.
Time management: spend time on the things you value or that help you reach your goals; plan, prioritise and delegate, and balance work and leisure.
Rational thinking: challenge distorted thinking and irrational beliefs, drive out intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts, and make positive statements.

example.q: A friend keeps asking Diya to do his assignments. Write an assertive reply and name the skill.
steps: Express your feeling and need clearly and respectfully.
Example: 'I understand you're busy, but I can't do your assignment. I can explain the topic if you like.'
Saying 'no' confidently without aggression = assertiveness.
example.answer: An honest, respectful 'no' — assertiveness.

learn.reallife: Many Indian boards and NGOs run life-skills education in schools, often based on the WHO list of life skills, so students learn to say no to risky peer pressure and manage exam time.

topics.title: Life skills: relationships, self-care and overcoming unhelpful habits

learn.hook: 'I'll start studying tomorrow.' Said every day for two weeks? Procrastination is one of three unhelpful habits that quietly pile up stress.
points: Improving relationships: communication is key — listening, expressing and explaining. Avoid jealousy and sulking; respect others' feelings.

Self-care: keeping ourselves healthy and relaxed so we are prepared physically and psychologically. Slow, deep abdominal breathing helps; we can also reduce environmental stressors such as noise, pollution, poor light and clutter.
Perfectionism: wanting everything done perfectly, which leads to tiredness and stress; perfectionists find it hard to relax and are critical of themselves and others.

Avoidance: putting issues 'under the carpet' and refusing to accept or face them. Procrastination: putting off what we know we must do ('I'll do it later'), often to avoid fear of failure or rejection.

For exam stress: plan with a timetable (time management), challenge catastrophic thoughts (rational thinking), keep sleep, food and exercise regular (self-care), talk to family or friends (relationships) and break tasks into small steps to beat procrastination.

example.q: Suggest a life-skills plan for Tanya, who is anxious about boards, studies late into the night, avoids difficult chapters and fights with her brother.
steps: Time management: a realistic timetable that tackles hard chapters in small chunks (beats avoidance and procrastination).
Self-care: fixed sleep time, healthy meals, short exercise breaks.
Rational thinking: replace 'I'll fail' with 'I've prepared — I can improve step by step'.
Relationships: calm talk with her brother; seek support from parents or a teacher.
example.answer: Combine time management, self-care, rational thinking and better relationships.

learn.reallife: Every board season, CBSE runs psychosocial counselling for students, and counsellors give the same advice: plan your time, sleep well, eat properly and talk to family instead of panicking.

topics.title: Positive health, stress buffers and social support

learn.hook: Health isn't just 'not being sick'. A body that works well, people who have your back, a sense of purpose — that's positive health.
points: Positive health includes a healthy body, good relationships, a sense of purpose in life, self-acceptance and resistance to illness.
Stress buffers protect us from the harmful effects of stress: a balanced diet, regular exercise, a positive attitude, positive thinking and social support.
Optimism — the tendency to expect the best possible outcomes — is linked with better psychological and physical well-being. Resilience is the ability to bounce back from adversity.

Social support is the existence and availability of people on whom we can rely, who show that they care for, value and love us. Perceived support (feeling supported) is strongly linked with well-being.

Types of social support: tangible (material help such as money, goods or services), informational (information about the stressful event, advice or tips) and emotional (reassurance that one is loved, valued and cared for).

example.q: Classify each kind of help to Arnav, who has broken his leg before exams: (a) his friend lends him notes, (b) a senior explains which chapters carry the most marks, (c) his grandmother reassures him that he is loved no matter the result.
steps: (a) Material help — notes = tangible support.
(b) Advice and information = informational support.
(c) Reassurance of love = emotional support.
example.answer: (a) Tangible, (b) Informational, (c) Emotional.

learn.reallife: When Kerala faced the 2018 floods, neighbours, fishermen and volunteers provided boats, food, information and comfort — all three types of social support at once. If you ever feel overwhelmed, talking to someone you trust or calling Tele-MANAS (14416) is a strong step.

topics.title: What is abnormal? The four Ds and stigma

learn.hook: Is a person who talks to herself on a phone headset 'abnormal'? Ten years ago people might have stared. Deciding what's a disorder is trickier than it looks.
points: Psychological disorders are patterns of behaviour, thought and emotion that cause significant distress and interfere with everyday functioning. 'Abnormal' literally means 'away from the normal'.

The four Ds: deviance (different, extreme, unusual or bizarre), distress (unpleasant and upsetting to the person and others), dysfunction (interfering with the ability to carry out daily activities in constructive ways) and danger (possibly dangerous to the person or others). Most people with psychological disorders are not dangerous.

Two approaches to abnormality: deviation from social norms (stated or unstated rules of a society) and maladaptive behaviour (behaviour that interferes with optimal functioning and growth). Many psychologists prefer the maladaptive view, since norms differ across cultures and times.

Stigma — negative labels and attitudes attached to mental illness — stops people from seeking help. Psychological disorders are not a personal failing; they are treatable, and seeking help is a sign of strength.
Using person-first, respectful language ('a person with depression', not 'a depressive') helps reduce stigma.

example.q: A student checks the gas knob 30 times every night, cannot sleep, feels deeply upset by it and is now missing school. Which of the four Ds apply?
steps: Repeating the check 30 times is unusual → deviance.
Feeling deeply upset → distress.
Missing school and sleep → dysfunction.
No risk of harm is described, so danger is not shown.
example.answer: Deviance, distress and dysfunction.

learn.reallife: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 protects the rights and dignity of persons with mental illness, and awareness drives in schools and colleges work to reduce stigma so people seek help early.

quiz.mistake: Assumes norms are universal.

A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: A is false: stigma discourages and delays help-seeking. R is true: negative labels make people afraid or ashamed.
steps: A: stigma encourages early treatment – false; it discourages and delays help-seeking.

topics.title: Historical views of abnormal behaviour

learn.hook: For centuries, people with mental illness were thought to be possessed. Today we talk about genes, thoughts and society. How did that shift happen?
points: Supernatural and magical approach: abnormal behaviour was blamed on evil spirits or magic; treatment included exorcism. A shaman (a person believed to have contact with supernatural forces) acted as the medium.
Biological or organic approach: ancient Greek thinkers such as Hippocrates, Socrates and Plato held that disorders have bodily causes, much like physical illnesses.
Psychological approach: problems arise from inadequacies in the way a person thinks, feels or perceives the world.

Middle Ages: demonology and superstition dominated. Renaissance: renewed humanism and curiosity about behaviour. Age of Reason and Enlightenment (17th–18th centuries): scientific thinking and more humane treatment.

Reform movement: asylums were reformed for humane care; later, deinstitutionalisation moved patients from large hospitals to community care. The modern interactional or biopsychosocial approach holds that biological, psychological and social factors all interact.

example.q: Arrange these views from earliest to most modern: biopsychosocial approach, demonology of the Middle Ages, Age of Reason and Enlightenment.
steps: Middle Ages came first — demonology.
The Age of Reason and Enlightenment (17th–18th centuries) came later.
The biopsychosocial approach is modern.
example.answer: Demonology → Age of Reason → biopsychosocial.

learn.reallife: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 promotes community-based care and rights for patients — part of the worldwide move from locked asylums to humane, community treatment.

topics.title: Classifying disorders and biological factors

learn.hook: Two doctors in Delhi and Chennai see patients with similar symptoms. How do they make sure they mean the same thing when they write 'depressive disorder'? They use shared classification systems.
points: The American Psychiatric Association publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders; its current edition is DSM-5.
The World Health Organization publishes the International Classification of Diseases. NCERT discusses ICD-10 (its chapter on mental and behavioural disorders); WHO has since brought ICD-11 into use.
Classification gives professionals a common language, helps in diagnosis and treatment planning, and supports research.

Biological factors: faulty genes, endocrine imbalances, malnutrition and injuries; and abnormal neurotransmitter activity. Low GABA activity is linked with anxiety, excess dopamine activity with schizophrenia, and low serotonin activity with depression. Brain structure abnormalities may also play a role.

example.q: A researcher finds that a person's brain shows unusually low activity of the neurotransmitter GABA. Which disorder group is this most associated with?
steps: GABA normally calms nerve activity.
Low GABA activity is linked with anxiety disorders.
example.answer: Anxiety disorders.

learn.reallife: AIIMS and NIMHANS psychiatrists diagnose using standard criteria like ICD and DSM so that research from Bengaluru can be compared with studies from London or Tokyo.

Low GABA → anxiety; excess dopamine → schizophrenia; low serotonin → depression

topics.title: Psychological and socio-cultural factors; diathesis–stress model

learn.hook: Two cousins carry the same family risk for depression. One faces years of hardship and develops it; the other doesn't. The diathesis–stress model explains why.
points: Psychodynamic model (the oldest and best known): behaviour comes from unconscious conflicts among id, ego and superego.

Behavioural model: abnormal behaviour results from learning maladaptive ways of behaving (through classical, operant or observational learning). Cognitive model: abnormal behaviour results from irrational assumptions and attitudes and unclear thinking.
Humanistic–existential model: focuses on broader aspects of human existence — humanists stress self-actualisation; existentialists stress freedom, responsibility and finding meaning.
Socio-cultural factors: war and violence, group stress, poverty and unemployment, prejudice and discrimination, family structure and communication, social networks, and societal labels and roles.

Diathesis–stress model: (1) a diathesis — a biological predisposition, which may be inherited; (2) this diathesis makes the person vulnerable to a disorder; (3) a pathogenic (harmful) stressor triggers the disorder. Both vulnerability and stressor are needed.

example.q: Meena has a family history of anxiety (inherited vulnerability). She develops severe anxiety only after losing her job and facing debts. Explain using the diathesis–stress model.
steps: Diathesis: inherited biological vulnerability for anxiety.
Pathogenic stressor: job loss and debts.
Vulnerability + stressor together produced the disorder.
example.answer: Her inherited diathesis interacted with severe stressors to trigger the disorder.

learn.reallife: After disasters like the 2001 Gujarat earthquake, not everyone developed lasting distress — studies point to the mix of personal vulnerability, the severity of the stress and the support available.

topics.title: Anxiety disorders

learn.hook: Everyone feels butterflies before a board exam. But when worry is constant, intense and not linked to anything specific, it may be an anxiety disorder.
points: Anxiety is a diffuse, vague, very unpleasant feeling of fear and apprehension. Symptoms can include rapid heart rate, shortness of breath, sweating, dizziness, loss of appetite, sleeplessness, frequent urination and tremors.

Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD): prolonged, vague, unexplained and intense fears not attached to any particular object; worry about the future, hypervigilance and motor tension (restlessness, inability to relax).

Panic disorder: recurrent panic attacks — abrupt surges of intense anxiety with shortness of breath, dizziness, trembling, palpitations, choking, nausea, chest pain, and fear of losing control or dying.

Phobias are irrational fears of specific objects, people or situations: specific phobias (most common, e.g. of animals or enclosed spaces), social anxiety disorder (intense fear and embarrassment when dealing with others) and agoraphobia (fear of entering unfamiliar situations; some avoid leaving home).
Separation anxiety disorder: children feel excessive anxiety or even panic when separated from parents or caregivers; they may be fussy, have tantrums or refuse to go to school.

example.q: A person feels sudden waves of terror with a pounding heart, chest pain and fear of dying, several times a month, without warning. Which disorder fits best?
steps: Sudden, recurrent attacks with intense physical symptoms = panic attacks.
Recurrent panic attacks define panic disorder.
GAD is continuous vague worry, not sudden attacks.
example.answer: Panic disorder.

learn.reallife: Many Indian students fear speaking in class or at interviews. When that fear becomes intense and disabling, it may be social anxiety disorder — very treatable with therapy. Tele-MANAS (14416) can guide people to help.

steps: Prolonged, vague, intense fears not tied to any object.
That is generalised anxiety disorder.
Answer: Generalised anxiety disorder
quiz.mistake: Confuses GAD with phobias, which have specific objects.

quiz.q: Recurrent, sudden attacks of intense terror with palpitations and fear of dying indicate:
quiz.explain: Panic disorder is defined by recurrent panic attacks.
steps: Sudden, recurrent attacks of terror with palpitations and fear of dying.
These are panic attacks; recurrent ones define panic disorder.
Answer: Panic disorder
quiz.mistake: Confuses sudden attacks with continuous worry.

quiz.q: Which is the most common type of phobia?
quiz.explain: Specific phobias are the most common.
steps: Phobias: specific phobia, social anxiety disorder, agoraphobia.
Specific phobias are the most common.
Answer: Specific phobia
quiz.mistake: Assumes agoraphobia is most common.

quiz.q: A child cries intensely, throws tantrums and refuses to go to school whenever separated from her mother. This suggests:
quiz.explain: Excessive distress on separation from caregivers marks separation anxiety disorder.
steps: Extreme distress, tantrums and school refusal on separation from her mother.
That suggests separation anxiety disorder.
Answer: Separation anxiety disorder
quiz.mistake: Labels the behaviour as conduct problems.

quiz.q: Fear of entering unfamiliar situations, leading some people to avoid leaving home, is:
quiz.explain: Agoraphobia is fear of unfamiliar situations.
steps: Fear of unfamiliar situations, so some avoid leaving home.
That is agoraphobia.
Answer: Agoraphobia
quiz.mistake: Confuses agoraphobia with social anxiety.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Any nervousness before an exam is an anxiety disorder.
Reason (R): Anxiety disorders involve intense, persistent anxiety that causes distress and interferes with functioning.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: ordinary, short-lived nervousness is normal. R is true: disorders involve intense, persistent anxiety with distress and dysfunction.
steps: A: any exam nervousness is a disorder – false; brief nervousness is normal.
R: disorders involve intense, persistent anxiety with distress and dysfunction – true.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Treats normal nervousness as a disorder.

quiz.q: Case: For over a year, Rekha worries constantly about everything — health, money, family — cannot relax, feels restless and is always on edge, though nothing specific is wrong. The most likely disorder is:
quiz.explain: Long-lasting, free-floating worry with motor tension and hypervigilance fits GAD.
steps: A year of constant worry about everything, restlessness and being on edge, with no specific cause.
Free-floating worry with motor tension fits GAD, not sudden panic attacks.
Answer: Generalised anxiety disorder
quiz.mistake: Picks panic disorder though no sudden attacks are described.

teach.ask: Gappu shakes: 'I'm scared of cats, and my friend panics suddenly for no reason. Are those the same thing?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Fear of cats is a specific phobia; sudden attacks are panic disorder; constant worry is GAD. Different disorders!
teach.nudge: What makes panic disorder different from a phobia?

revise.summary: Anxiety is diffuse fear and apprehension. Anxiety disorders include generalised anxiety disorder (free-floating worry), panic disorder (recurrent panic attacks), phobias (specific, social anxiety, agoraphobia) and separation anxiety disorder.
remember: GAD: prolonged, vague fears not tied to an object; hypervigilance, motor tension
Panic disorder: recurrent sudden panic attacks
Specific phobia is the most common
Agoraphobia: fear of unfamiliar situations
traps: GAD is continuous worry, not sudden attacks
Ordinary short-lived exam nervousness is not a disorder
Agoraphobia is not the same as social anxiety disorder

topics.title: Obsessive-compulsive, related and trauma disorders

learn.hook: People joke 'I'm so OCD' about tidy desks. Real OCD isn't a quirk — it's distressing thoughts and rituals that can take hours each day.
points: Obsessive behaviour is the inability to stop thinking about a particular idea or topic; these thoughts are unwanted, unpleasant and often shameful to the person.

Compulsive behaviour is the need to perform certain behaviours repeatedly, such as counting, ordering, checking, touching and washing. In obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), obsessions and compulsions take a lot of time and interfere with life.
Related disorders include hoarding disorder (difficulty discarding possessions), trichotillomania (repeated hair-pulling) and excoriation (repeated skin-picking).
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) can follow traumatic events such as natural disasters, serious accidents or violence.
PTSD symptoms include recurrent dreams or nightmares, flashbacks, impaired concentration and emotional numbing. Treatment and support help people recover.

example.q: Arjun keeps thinking his hands are contaminated (1) and washes them 40 times a day (2), spending hours and missing classes. Label (1) and (2).
steps: (1) An unwanted, recurring thought = obsession.
(2) A repeated action to reduce the anxiety = compulsion.
Together, causing distress and dysfunction, they suggest OCD.
example.answer: (1) Obsession, (2) Compulsion.

learn.reallife: After the 2013 Uttarakhand floods, mental health teams worked with survivors who had nightmares and flashbacks — classic PTSD symptoms — showing why disaster relief needs psychological care too.

That is obsessive behaviour.

Answer: Obsessive behaviour
quiz.mistake: Confuses obsession (thought) with compulsion (action).

quiz.q: The need to perform certain behaviours over and over, like checking or washing, is:
quiz.explain: Compulsions are repeated actions.
steps: Repeatedly checking or washing.
That is compulsive behaviour.
Answer: Compulsive behaviour
quiz.mistake: Calls the action an obsession.

quiz.explain: Trichotillomania is a hair-pulling disorder.

Excoriation is skin-picking.
Answer: Trichotillomania
quiz.mistake: Mixes it with excoriation (skin-picking).

quiz.q: PTSD typically follows:
options: A traumatic event such as a disaster or serious accident
quiz.explain: PTSD develops after traumatic events.
steps: PTSD follows traumatic events such as disasters, serious accidents or violence.
Answer: A traumatic event such as a disaster or serious accident
quiz.mistake: Thinks any stress leads to PTSD.

quiz.q: Which is a symptom of PTSD?
quiz.explain: PTSD involves flashbacks, nightmares, poor concentration and emotional numbing.
steps: PTSD symptoms: nightmares, flashbacks, poor concentration, emotional numbing.
Answer: Flashbacks and emotional numbing
quiz.mistake: Picks symptoms of mania or schizophrenia.

quiz.q: Difficulty discarding possessions, leading to severe clutter, is characteristic of:
quiz.explain: Hoarding disorder is an obsessive-compulsive related disorder.
steps: Difficulty discarding possessions, leading to clutter.
That is hoarding disorder.
Answer: Hoarding disorder
quiz.mistake: Picks an unrelated disorder.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Being neat and organised does not mean a person has OCD.
Reason (R): OCD involves unwanted obsessions and compulsions that cause distress and take up a lot of time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; OCD requires distressing, time-consuming obsessions and compulsions, not just neatness.
steps: A: neatness does not mean OCD – true.
R: OCD involves distressing, time-consuming obsessions and compulsions – true.
Since OCD needs these, neatness alone is not OCD.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Uses the casual meaning of 'OCD'.

quiz.q: Case: Months after a severe bus accident, Farah has nightmares about it, cannot concentrate and feels emotionally 'numb'. The most likely disorder is:
quiz.explain: Nightmares, poor concentration and numbing after trauma fit PTSD.
steps: Nightmares, poor concentration and numbness months after a bus accident.
These follow trauma and fit PTSD.
Answer: Post-traumatic stress disorder
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the link with the traumatic event.

teach.ask: Gappu worries: 'I keep thinking my nest is dirty and I clean it all day. Is that an obsession or a compulsion?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The worrying thought is an obsession, the cleaning is a compulsion — and real OCD deserves real help!
teach.nudge: Which part is the thought and which is the action?

revise.summary: OCD involves unwanted recurring thoughts (obsessions) and repeated actions (compulsions) that take time and disrupt life. Related disorders are hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation. PTSD follows trauma, with nightmares, flashbacks, poor concentration and numbing.
remember: Obsession: unwanted recurring thought
Compulsion: repeated action such as checking or washing
Trichotillomania: hair-pulling; excoriation: skin-picking
PTSD: nightmares, flashbacks, poor concentration, emotional numbing
traps: Don't swap obsession (thought) and compulsion (action)
Being neat is not OCD
Trichotillomania is hair-pulling, not skin-picking

topics.title: Somatic symptom and dissociative disorders

learn.hook: A person suddenly cannot move an arm, yet every medical test is normal. Another forgets who they are and turns up in a different city. The mind can affect the body and memory in surprising ways.
points: Somatic symptom and related disorders involve psychological difficulties expressed as physical symptoms without an adequate biological cause.

Somatic symptom disorder: persistent body-related symptoms with heavy preoccupation, constant worry about health and frequent visits to doctors. Illness anxiety disorder: persistent preoccupation with the possibility of having or developing a serious illness, with frequent body-checking.

Conversion disorder: reported loss of part or all of some basic body functions (for example, paralysis, blindness, deafness or difficulty walking) with no physical cause, often after a stressful experience and sometimes suddenly.

Dissociation is a severance of the connections between ideas and emotions, involving feelings of unreality, estrangement and sometimes a shift in identity. Dissociative amnesia: extensive but selective memory loss with no known organic cause; dissociative fugue (a part of it) involves unexpected travel away from home and assuming a new identity.

Dissociative identity disorder (once called multiple personality): the person assumes alternate personalities that may or may not be aware of each other. Depersonalisation/derealisation: a dreamlike state where the person feels separated from self and from reality.

example.q: After a terrifying event, a man cannot remember anything about the week it happened, but medical scans show no brain injury. Which disorder is most likely?
steps: Memory loss is selective — focused on a stressful period.
No organic cause is found.
This fits dissociative amnesia.
example.answer: Dissociative amnesia.

learn.reallife: Doctors in Indian hospitals often see patients with physical complaints that tests can't explain; a referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist is part of good care, not a dismissal of the patient's suffering.

pairs: Persistent bodily symptoms with excessive preoccupation
Constant worry about having a serious illness

quiz.mistake: Confuses them with psychotic or OCD symptoms.

quiz.q: Persistent worry about having a serious illness, with frequent body-checking, is:
quiz.explain: Illness anxiety disorder centres on fear of having serious illness.

Answer: Illness anxiety disorder

quiz.q: A sudden loss of vision after a stressful event, with no physical cause found, suggests:
quiz.explain: Conversion disorder involves loss of basic body functions without physical cause.

Answer: Conversion disorder

quiz.explain: Dissociation involves a split between ideas and emotions, with feelings of unreality.
steps: Dissociation = a severance of the connections between ideas and emotions.
It brings feelings of unreality.
Answer: A severance of the connections between ideas and emotions
quiz.mistake: Confuses dissociation with compulsions.

quiz.q: Dissociative fugue involves:

quiz.explain: Fugue is a form of dissociative amnesia with travel and new identity.

quiz.mistake: Confuses fugue with agoraphobia.

quiz.q: A person who feels as if she is watching herself in a dream and the world seems unreal is experiencing:
quiz.explain: This disorder involves a sense of separation from self and reality.
steps: Feeling like watching oneself in a dream, the world unreal.
That is depersonalisation/derealisation.
Answer: Depersonalisation/derealisation
quiz.mistake: Calls it multiple personality.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In dissociative amnesia, a person may forget specific stressful events.
Reason (R): Dissociative identity disorder was earlier called multiple personality.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the old name of DID does not explain memory loss in dissociative amnesia.
steps: A: dissociative amnesia can involve forgetting specific stressful events – true.
R: DID was earlier called multiple personality – true.
The old name of DID does not explain amnesia.
So both are true, but R is not the correct explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Assumes any true fact about dissociation explains A.

quiz.q: Case: Over two years, Mr. Sharma visits many doctors for stomach pain and headaches; tests are normal but he remains highly preoccupied and worried about his symptoms. The most likely disorder is:
quiz.explain: Persistent bodily symptoms with excessive preoccupation and doctor visits fit somatic symptom disorder.
steps: Two years of stomach pain and headaches, normal tests, heavy worry and many doctor visits.
Persistent bodily symptoms with preoccupation = somatic symptom disorder.
No body function is lost, so it is not conversion.
Answer: Somatic symptom disorder
quiz.mistake: Picks conversion disorder although no body function is lost.

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in confusion: 'My friend can't fly, but the vet says his wings are fine! Another forgot his own name. What's going on?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The flying problem is conversion disorder; forgetting his name is dissociative amnesia. The mind is powerful!
teach.nudge: What is it called when someone loses a body function without any physical cause?

revise.summary: Somatic symptom disorders turn psychological difficulty into physical symptoms (somatic symptom, illness anxiety, conversion). Dissociative disorders break links between ideas and emotions: amnesia, fugue, dissociative identity disorder and depersonalisation/derealisation.

Matching a case to the disorder

Illness anxiety: fear of having a serious illness
Fugue: unexpected travel and new identity
DID: alternate personalities (once multiple personality)

Dissociative amnesia has no organic cause

topics.title: Depressive and bipolar disorders; preventing suicide

learn.hook: Feeling sad after a bad result is human. Feeling empty, tired and hopeless for weeks, losing interest in everything you used to love — that may be depression, and it deserves care.
points: Major depressive disorder: a period (at least two weeks) of depressed mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure in most activities, along with other symptoms.

Other symptoms include change in body weight, persistent sleep problems, tiredness, inability to think clearly, agitation or greatly slowed behaviour, excessive guilt or worthlessness, and thoughts of death.
Risk factors: genetic make-up, age, gender (women are more likely than men to report depressive disorders), negative life events and lack of social support.

Bipolar I disorder: manic and depressive episodes alternate, sometimes with periods of normal mood in between (once called manic-depressive disorder). Mania involves euphoria, extreme activity, excessive talkativeness, distractibility and poor judgement.

Suicide prevention: warning signs can include talking about wanting to die, withdrawing from friends and activities, sudden mood changes and giving away possessions. Take every sign seriously — listen without judging, stay with the person, tell a trusted adult and connect them to professional help such as Tele-MANAS (14416). Asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts does not put the idea in their head.

example.q: A person alternates between weeks of extreme energy, non-stop talking and risky spending, and weeks of deep sadness and exhaustion. What disorder does this pattern suggest?
steps: High-energy, euphoric, talkative episodes = mania.
Periods of deep sadness = depressive episodes.
Alternating mania and depression = bipolar I disorder.
example.answer: Bipolar I disorder.

learn.reallife: Tele-MANAS (dial 14416 or 1-800-891-4416) is India's free, 24×7 mental health helpline in many Indian languages. If you or a friend ever feel hopeless, reaching out is a brave, important first step.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

topics.title: Schizophrenia: nature and positive symptoms

learn.hook: Imagine hearing voices no one else hears, or being sure strangers are spying on you. For people with schizophrenia these experiences feel completely real.
points: Schizophrenia is a group of psychotic disorders in which personal, social and occupational functioning deteriorate due to disturbed thought processes, strange perceptions, unusual emotional states and motor abnormalities.

Positive symptoms are 'pathological excesses' or bizarre additions. Delusions are false beliefs held firmly on inadequate grounds and not changed by rational argument: persecution (most common — being plotted against or spied on), reference (special personal meaning in others' actions or events), grandeur (being specially empowered or important) and control (feelings, thoughts and actions controlled by others).

Hallucinations are perceptions without external stimuli. Auditory hallucinations (hearing voices) are the most common; others are tactile (tingling, burning), somatic (something happening inside the body), visual, gustatory (taste) and olfactory (smell).

Formal thought disorder: loosening of associations or derailment (rapid shifts between unrelated topics), neologisms (made-up words), perseveration (persistent, inappropriate repetition of the same thoughts) and clang (rhyming words).
Inappropriate affect: emotions unsuited to the situation, such as laughing on hearing sad news.

example.q: A person insists that a TV news anchor is sending him secret messages meant only for him. Which type of delusion is this?
steps: He gives special personal meaning to events (the news broadcast).
That is a delusion of reference.
example.answer: Delusion of reference.

learn.reallife: NIMHANS and community programmes like the District Mental Health Programme help people with schizophrenia get medicines, therapy and family support so they can live in their communities.

quiz.mistake: Confuses delusions with hallucinations.

quiz.explain: Delusions of persecution are the most common.

Answer: Grandeur

Answer: Auditory

Answer: Somatic hallucination

Assertion (A): Laughing on hearing that a close relative has died can be a symptom of schizophrenia.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

steps: A: laughing on hearing of a death can be a symptom – true.
R: inappropriate affect means emotions unsuited to the situation – true.
Laughing at sad news is inappropriate affect.

Answer: Neologism

teach.praise: Tweet. Hearing voices is a hallucination; believing she's being spied on is a delusion of persecution. She needs care, not fear.
teach.nudge: What's the difference between a delusion and a hallucination?

revise.summary: Schizophrenia is a group of psychotic disorders with deteriorating functioning. Positive symptoms (excesses) include delusions (persecution, reference, grandeur, control), hallucinations (auditory most common), formal thought disorder and inappropriate affect.
focus: Formal thought disorder: derailment, neologisms, perseveration, clang
remember: Delusion: firmly held false belief
Persecution: most common delusion; auditory: most common hallucination
Somatic hallucination: inside the body; tactile: on the skin
Neologism: made-up word
traps: Don't confuse delusions (beliefs) with hallucinations (perceptions)
Somatic is not tactile
Reference means special personal meaning, not grandeur

topics.title: Schizophrenia: negative and psychomotor symptoms, and causes

learn.hook: Positive symptoms add something — voices, false beliefs. Negative symptoms take something away — speech, emotion, motivation. Both matter for recovery.
points: Negative symptoms are 'pathological deficits': poverty of speech (alogia — reduced speech and speech content), blunted and flat affect (reduced or no emotional expression), loss of volition (avolition — apathy and inability to start or complete a course of action) and social withdrawal.

Psychomotor symptoms (catatonia): catatonic stupor (motionless and silent for long periods), catatonic rigidity (maintaining a rigid, upright posture for hours) and catatonic posturing (holding awkward, bizarre positions for long periods).
Biological causes: the dopamine hypothesis (excess dopamine activity) and brain structure abnormalities; genetic factors increase risk.

Psychological and socio-cultural causes include family stress, faulty communication patterns and stressful life conditions. In line with the diathesis–stress model, vulnerability and stressors interact.

example.q: Classify each: (a) hearing voices, (b) speaking very little with almost no content, (c) showing no facial expression even at happy news, (d) standing in one odd position for hours.
steps: (a) An excess experience → positive symptom (hallucination).
(b) Reduced speech → negative symptom (alogia).
(c) Reduced emotional expression → negative symptom (flat affect).
(d) Odd motor behaviour → psychomotor symptom (catatonic posturing).
example.answer: (a) Positive, (b) Negative, (c) Negative, (d) Psychomotor.

learn.reallife: Rehabilitation programmes in India, such as those at NIMHANS, focus heavily on negative symptoms — helping people rebuild motivation, social skills and daily routines.

quiz.explain: Reduced emotion and motivation are negative symptoms; schizophrenia does not require hallucinations at every point.

Answer: She mainly shows negative symptoms such as flat affect and avolition
quiz.mistake: Assumes hallucinations must always be present.

teach.ask: Gappu puzzles: 'Why are some symptoms called negative? Aren't all symptoms negative?'

teach.nudge: Can you give one example of a negative symptom?

revise.summary: Negative symptoms are deficits: alogia, flat affect, avolition and social withdrawal. Psychomotor symptoms include catatonic stupor, rigidity and posturing. Causes include excess dopamine, brain abnormalities, genes and family and life stress.

Biological and psychological causes of schizophrenia

Catatonic stupor: motionless and silent; rigidity: rigid posture; posturing: odd positions
Dopamine hypothesis: excess dopamine

topics.title: Neurodevelopmental disorders

learn.hook: A brilliant child who struggles to read the board, another who can't sit still, a third who lines up toys perfectly but avoids eye contact — each may need a different kind of support.
points: Neurodevelopmental disorders first appear in early development and affect functioning in daily life, school and relationships.

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has two main features: inattention (difficulty sustaining attention, easily distracted, not following instructions) and hyperactivity–impulsivity (difficulty waiting or resisting urges, blurting answers, constant motion, fidgeting).

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD): varying degrees of difficulty in social interaction and communication, with restricted interests and a strong need for routine and repetitive behaviours (such as rocking).

Intellectual disability: below-average intellectual functioning (IQ of about 70 or below) together with deficits in adaptive behaviour (communication, self-care, social skills, home living), manifested before 18.

Specific learning disorder: difficulty in perceiving or processing information efficiently and accurately, seen in reading, writing or maths skills well below the expected level for the child's age, starting in the early school years.

example.q: A 7-year-old with average intelligence reads far below grade level, mixes up letters and struggles with spelling despite good teaching. Which disorder is most likely?
steps: Intelligence is average, so intellectual disability is unlikely.
The difficulty is specific to reading and spelling.
This fits specific learning disorder.
example.answer: Specific learning disorder.

learn.reallife: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 recognises specific learning disabilities and autism spectrum disorder, and CBSE allows accommodations such as extra time and scribes for eligible students.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Both are true; because the problem is skill-specific, general intelligence may be normal.
