topics.title: Disruptive, conduct and feeding–eating disorders

learn.hook: One teen argues with every adult rule. Another hurts animals and steals. A third sees herself as overweight when she's dangerously thin. Very different problems, all needing understanding and help.
points: Oppositional defiant disorder (ODD): age-inappropriate amounts of stubbornness, irritability, defiance, disobedience and hostility. Unlike conduct disorder, it does not typically involve aggression towards people or animals or destruction of property.

Conduct disorder: age-inappropriate actions and attitudes that violate family expectations, social norms and the personal or property rights of others — aggression towards people or animals, property damage, deceitfulness, theft and serious rule-breaking.
Types of aggressive behaviour: verbal (name-calling, swearing), physical (hitting, fighting), hostile (aimed at injuring others) and proactive (dominating and bullying without provocation).

Anorexia nervosa: a distorted body image — seeing oneself as overweight — with refusal to eat, compulsive exercise and unusual eating habits, leading to dangerous weight loss. Bulimia nervosa: eating excessive amounts followed by purging, with feelings of shame afterwards.

Binge eating disorder: frequent episodes of out-of-control eating, often faster than usual and until uncomfortably full, without purging. Eating disorders are serious but treatable; early help matters.

example.q: Compare: Riya (body weight very low, believes she is fat, refuses meals) and Simran (normal weight, eats large amounts secretly then purges, feels ashamed).
steps: Riya: distorted body image, food refusal, very low weight → anorexia nervosa.
Simran: binge eating followed by purging → bulimia nervosa.
Key difference: anorexia involves restriction and very low weight; bulimia involves binge–purge cycles.
example.answer: Riya: anorexia nervosa; Simran: bulimia nervosa.

learn.reallife: Indian teens face heavy pressure from social media 'body goals'. School counsellors now watch for signs of eating disorders and encourage early, non-judgemental support.

topics.title: Substance-related and addictive disorders

learn.hook: 'Just once won't hurt.' But some substances change the brain so that 'once' turns into 'need'. Understanding tolerance and withdrawal explains why addiction is so hard to escape.
points: Substance use disorders include substance dependence (intense craving with tolerance and withdrawal) and substance abuse (recurrent use with significant harmful consequences). Tolerance: needing more of a substance to get the same effect. Withdrawal: unpleasant physical and psychological symptoms when use stops or reduces.

Alcohol: regular heavy drinkers come to rely on alcohol to face difficult situations; it eventually harms family and social relationships, ability to think and work, and physical health (such as liver damage). Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant.

Heroin (an opioid): use quickly interferes with social and occupational functioning; most users develop dependence with tolerance and withdrawal. Overdose can dangerously slow breathing and can be fatal.

Cocaine (a stimulant): regular use can lead to abuse, poor functioning in relationships and work, and problems with short-term memory and attention. Withdrawal brings depression, fatigue, sleep problems, irritability and anxiety.
Help is available: de-addiction centres, counselling and helplines. The national toll-free de-addiction helpline is 14446, and Tele-MANAS (14416) can also guide people.

example.q: Vikas once felt relaxed after one drink; now he needs four drinks for the same effect, and when he stops he feels shaky, anxious and sweaty. Which two features of dependence are shown?
steps: Needing more for the same effect = tolerance.
Shakiness, anxiety and sweating on stopping = withdrawal.
example.answer: Tolerance and withdrawal.

learn.reallife: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan runs awareness drives in schools and colleges, and the national de-addiction helpline (14446) connects people to counselling and treatment.

topics.title: Nature, characteristics and goals of psychotherapy

learn.hook: Talking to a friend helps. So why train for years to become a therapist? Because psychotherapy is a systematic, theory-based process — not just a chat.
points: Psychotherapy is a voluntary relationship between the one seeking treatment (the client) and the one who treats (the therapist). Its purpose is to help the client solve psychological problems.

Characteristics: (1) systematic application of principles from theories of therapy; (2) only trained persons with practical, supervised experience practise it; (3) the therapeutic situation involves a therapist and a client who seeks help; (4) the relationship is confidential, interpersonal and dynamic.
Goals (part 1): reinforcing the client's resolve for betterment; lessening emotional pressure; unfolding the potential for positive growth; modifying habits.

Goals (part 2): changing thinking patterns; increasing self-awareness; improving interpersonal relations and communication; facilitating decision-making; becoming aware of one's choices in life; relating to one's social environment in a more creative and self-aware manner.

example.q: A friend says, 'Therapy is just talking — my uncle gives great advice too.' Give two characteristics that make psychotherapy different.
steps: It applies principles from established theories systematically.
Only trained, supervised professionals practise it.
It is a confidential, professional relationship focused on the client's goals.
example.answer: Psychotherapy is theory-based, systematic, done by trained professionals and confidential — unlike casual advice.

learn.reallife: India's Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) registers clinical psychologists, ensuring that people offering therapy have proper training and supervision.

topics.title: The therapeutic relationship

learn.hook: 'I feel sorry for you' versus 'I can feel what this is like for you.' One is sympathy, the other empathy — and therapists need the second.
points: The therapeutic relationship (alliance) has two major components. It is contractual: two willing individuals enter a partnership to help the client overcome problems. It is of limited duration: it lasts until the client can deal with problems and take control of life.
The client must be able to trust the therapist; what the client shares is kept confidential, and the therapist must not exploit this trust.
The therapist shows unconditional positive regard (warmth and acceptance regardless of what the client says) and empathy for the client.

Empathy: understanding the client's situation from the client's perspective, as if one were in their place. Sympathy: compassion and pity for another's suffering, but without feeling what they feel. Intellectual understanding: cold — one understands the facts but feels neither.
The relationship must remain professional, with clear boundaries.

example.q: A client says she feels like a failure after losing her job. Write one empathic, one sympathetic and one intellectual response.
steps: Empathic: 'It sounds like losing the job has shaken your sense of worth; that must feel heavy.'
Sympathetic: 'Oh, poor you, that's so sad.'
Intellectual: 'Job losses are common in this economy.'
example.answer: Only the first truly enters the client's perspective — empathy.

learn.reallife: Indian therapy guidelines stress confidentiality and boundaries — a therapist may not, for instance, start a business partnership with a client, because it would compromise the professional relationship.

topics.title: Types of therapies and bases of classification

learn.hook: If two therapists treat the same anxious client, one might teach relaxation and another explore the meaning of the client's life. How do we compare such different approaches?
points: Psychotherapies fall into three broad groups: psychodynamic, behaviour and existential (humanistic-existential) therapies. Historically, psychodynamic therapy emerged first, then behaviour therapy; existential therapies, called the 'third force', emerged last. (Details of psychodynamic therapy are not part of the rationalised syllabus.)

Therapies are compared on six parameters: (1) what is the cause of the problem, (2) how did the cause come into existence, (3) what is the chief method of treatment, (4) what is the nature of the therapeutic relationship, (5) what is the chief benefit to the client, (6) what is the duration of treatment.

For example, behaviour therapy sees the cause as faulty learning, uses behavioural techniques, and usually runs for a few months; humanistic-existential therapy sees the cause as lack of meaning and alienation, and aims at personal growth.

example.q: Use the six parameters to describe behaviour therapy for a child's fear of dogs.
steps: Cause: a learned fear response.
How it arose: faulty conditioning, e.g. after a dog chased the child.
Method: behavioural techniques such as systematic desensitisation.
Relationship: therapist guides and trains the client.
Benefit: fear reduced, normal behaviour restored.
Duration: usually a few months.
example.answer: Each parameter can be answered, allowing comparison with other therapies.

learn.reallife: Just as a doctor compares medicines by cause, method, side effects and duration, NCERT compares therapies on six parameters — a handy table for board answers.

topics.title: Behaviour therapy: principles and behavioural analysis

learn.hook: A child throws a tantrum at dinner every night. A behaviour therapist doesn't ask about his dreams — she asks: what happens just before, and just after?
points: Behaviour therapies hold that psychological distress arises from faulty behaviour or thought patterns learned in the past. The focus is on the client's present behaviours; the past matters only to understand how the faulty pattern began.

Behavioural analysis identifies malfunctioning behaviours, the faulty learning behind them, the antecedent factors (what triggers them) and the maintaining factors (what keeps them going). It looks at antecedents, the maladaptive behaviour and its consequences.

Antecedent operations control behaviour by changing something that precedes it. An establishing operation increases or decreases the reinforcing value of a consequence; for example, if a child fusses at dinner, giving him less food at tea-time makes him hungrier at dinner, increasing the value of dinner and reducing fussing.
Consequent operations change the consequences that follow a behaviour (rewarding wanted behaviour, not rewarding unwanted behaviour).
Relaxation procedures reduce arousal; once the client is calm, behavioural techniques can be applied more effectively.

example.q: Analyse Aryan's tantrums: they start when his favourite cartoon is switched off for homework (A), he screams (B), and his parents switch the TV back on (C). What keeps the tantrum going?
steps: Antecedent: TV switched off.
Behaviour: screaming tantrum.
Consequence: TV switched back on — this rewards the tantrum.
The consequence is the maintaining factor.
example.answer: The reward of getting the TV back maintains the tantrums.

learn.reallife: Parents in many Indian homes unknowingly reward tantrums by giving in. Behaviour therapists teach them to change the consequence — a simple shift with big results.

topics.title: Reinforcement, aversive conditioning and token economy

learn.hook: Stars on a chart, a favourite dish after homework, ignoring a sulk — these everyday tricks are real behaviour therapy techniques.
points: Negative reinforcement (as NCERT describes it): an undesired response is followed by an outcome that is painful or not liked, so the person learns the response that avoids it — for example, going out in winter without woollens brings the cold, so one teaches oneself to wear woollen clothes.

Aversive conditioning: repeated association of an undesired response with an aversive (unpleasant) consequence, so the behaviour becomes unpleasant and decreases. For example, in treatment for alcohol dependence, the smell of alcohol is repeatedly paired with a mild unpleasant stimulus under professional supervision.
Positive reinforcement: if an adaptive behaviour occurs rarely, it is followed by a reward (for example, a favourite dish when homework is done regularly).
Token economy: a person earns a token each time a wanted behaviour occurs; tokens are collected and exchanged for a reward such as an outing or a treat.

Differential reinforcement: increasing wanted behaviour and reducing unwanted behaviour at the same time — either by positively reinforcing the wanted behaviour and following the unwanted one with a disliked outcome (negative reinforcement, in NCERT's terms), or, less painfully, by reinforcing the wanted behaviour and ignoring the unwanted one (e.g., parents take a girl to the film when she doesn't sulk, and ignore her when she sulks).

example.q: Design a token economy for residents of a rehabilitation centre who rarely make their beds.
steps: Target behaviour: making the bed every morning.
Each time it is done, give one token.
Tokens can be exchanged, e.g. 10 tokens for an outing or a special treat.
Gradually, the behaviour increases because it is reinforced.
example.answer: Tokens are given for each instance of the wanted behaviour and exchanged for rewards.

learn.reallife: Many Indian schools use house points or star charts for punctuality and cleanliness — a classroom version of the token economy.

topics.title: Systematic desensitisation and modelling

learn.hook: Scared of heights? A therapist won't push you off a cliff. She'll start with a picture of a stool — while you're deeply relaxed — and climb slowly from there.
points: Systematic desensitisation, introduced by Joseph Wolpe, treats phobias and irrational fears.

Steps: (1) the client is interviewed to identify fear-provoking situations; (2) together they build a hierarchy of anxiety-provoking stimuli, with the least anxiety-provoking at the bottom; (3) the client is relaxed; (4) the client imagines the least anxiety-provoking situation and stops if any tension is felt; (5) over sessions, the client moves up the hierarchy while staying relaxed.

It works on the principle of reciprocal inhibition: two mutually opposing forces (relaxation and anxiety) cannot exist at the same time; the stronger relaxation response inhibits the weaker anxiety response.

Modelling: the client learns to behave in a certain way by observing a role model. Vicarious learning means learning by observing others being reinforced. The therapist may act as the model and reinforce small changes towards the desired behaviour.

example.q: Build a hierarchy for Ritu, who fears dogs, from least to most anxiety-provoking: touching a dog, seeing a picture of a dog, a dog in the next room, a dog across the street.
steps: Least: seeing a picture.
Next: a dog across the street.
Next: a dog in the next room.
Most: touching a dog.
She moves up only while staying relaxed.
example.answer: Picture → dog across the street → dog in next room → touching a dog.

learn.reallife: Fear of flying is common among first-time flyers in India. Therapists use desensitisation — videos of airports, then sitting in a parked plane — before an actual flight.

topics.title: Cognitive therapy: Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy

learn.hook: A friend doesn't reply to your message. You feel hurt. But was it the unanswered message — or your belief 'She must hate me' — that hurt?
points: Cognitive therapies locate the cause of psychological distress in irrational thoughts and beliefs.

Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Therapy (RET): irrational beliefs mediate between antecedent events and their consequences. ABC model: A = antecedent event, B = belief, C = consequence (emotions and behaviour).
The first step is the ABC analysis: identify the antecedent events that caused distress and the irrational beliefs behind them, through client interviews.

Irrational beliefs are marked by 'musts' and 'shoulds' (e.g., 'I must be loved by everyone', 'I should never fail'), and by awfulising. They distort how the antecedent event is perceived, producing negative emotions and behaviours.

The therapist refutes irrational beliefs through non-directive questioning that is gentle, without probing or being directive, making the client think deeper about their assumptions and gradually adopt rational beliefs.

example.q: Apply the ABC model: Kunal scores 70% in a test (A), believes 'I must always score above 90% or I'm worthless' (B), and feels hopeless and stops studying (C).
steps: A (antecedent): 70% in the test.
B (belief): an irrational 'must' — 'I must always score above 90%.'
C (consequence): hopelessness and avoidance.
Therapy targets B, not A: replace it with 'I'd like higher marks, but 70% doesn't make me worthless.'
example.answer: A = 70% score; B = irrational 'must' belief; C = hopelessness — change B to change C.

learn.reallife: Coaching-centre students in Kota often carry beliefs like 'I must crack the exam this year or my life is over'. Counsellors use RET-style questioning to soften these musts.

topics.title: Beck's cognitive therapy and CBT

learn.hook: 'Nobody likes me.' 'I'm stupid.' Thoughts that pop up automatically can feel like facts. Aaron Beck taught people to question them.
points: Aaron Beck: childhood experiences provide basic cognitive schemas or core beliefs (e.g., 'I am unwanted'). Critical incidents later in life activate these core schemas.

Activated core schemas produce negative automatic thoughts — persistent irrational thoughts such as 'Nobody loves me', 'I am ugly', 'I am stupid'. Cognitive distortions are ways of thinking that distort reality in a negative way; repeated, they lead to anxiety and depression.

Therapy uses gentle, non-threatening disputation of beliefs and thoughts through Socratic questioning, such as 'Why should everyone love you?' or 'What does it mean to you to succeed?' The client discovers contradictions in their own thinking and changes their views.

Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) is a short, effective therapy for many disorders such as anxiety, depression and panic attacks. It combines cognitive therapy with behavioural techniques and follows a biopsychosocial approach — relaxation for the biological, cognitive and behavioural methods for the psychological, and environmental changes for the social.

example.q: Riddhi was often told as a child that she was a burden (core schema: 'I am unwanted'). Years later, a friend cancels plans and she thinks 'Nobody wants me around.' Identify each part using Beck's model.
steps: Childhood experience → core schema 'I am unwanted'.
Critical incident: friend cancels plans.
Activated schema produces a negative automatic thought: 'Nobody wants me around.'
A therapist would use Socratic questions: 'What other reasons might she have had to cancel?'
example.answer: Core schema → critical incident → negative automatic thought, challenged by Socratic questioning.

learn.reallife: CBT is now offered in many Indian hospitals and through digital platforms; NIMHANS has trained counsellors to deliver CBT-based support for depression and anxiety.

topics.title: Humanistic-existential therapies: logotherapy, client-centred and Gestalt

learn.hook: Victor Frankl survived a Nazi concentration camp and came out with a powerful idea: people can endure almost anything if they find meaning in it.
points: Humanistic-existential therapies see psychological distress as arising from loneliness, alienation and an inability to find meaning and fulfilment. People have an innate need for personal growth and self-actualisation. The therapist provides a permissive, non-judgemental, accepting atmosphere and acts as a facilitator; the client is responsible for the success of therapy.

Logotherapy (Victor Frankl): 'logos' means soul, so logotherapy is 'treatment of the soul'. It helps clients find meaning even in painful experiences (meaning-making). Existential anxiety is neurotic anxiety of spiritual origin, arising from problems about the meaning of life. Paradoxical intention encourages clients to deliberately wish for or do the very thing they fear, often with humour, to weaken anxiety.

Client-centred therapy (Carl Rogers): the therapist shows empathy, warmth and unconditional positive regard, and uses reflection of feelings and clarification of the client's thoughts. It is non-directive, helping clients reconnect with their feelings and grow.

Gestalt therapy (Frederick 'Fritz' Perls with Laura Perls): 'gestalt' means whole. Its goal is to increase self-awareness and self-acceptance; clients learn to recognise bodily processes and emotions blocked from awareness, and may act out fantasies about feelings and conflicts. It can be used in groups.

example.q: A client says, 'I feel nobody at home understands me.' What would a client-centred therapist say?
steps: Reflect the feeling back without judging or advising.
'You're feeling lonely and unheard by your family.'
This shows empathy and lets the client explore further.
example.answer: A reflection such as 'You feel lonely and unheard at home' — showing empathy and acceptance.

learn.reallife: Meaning-centred counselling inspired by logotherapy is used with patients facing serious illness in palliative care centres, helping them find purpose in family, relationships and helping others.

topics.title: Alternative therapies: yoga and meditation

learn.hook: International Yoga Day draws millions every 21 June. Beyond flexibility, research at Indian institutes shows breathing-based yoga can help with depression.
points: Alternative therapies are alternatives to conventional drug treatment or psychotherapy — for example, yoga, meditation, acupuncture and herbal remedies. They are often used alongside, not instead of, professional treatment.
Yoga is an ancient Indian technique described in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. As therapy it may use asanas (body postures), pranayama (breathing practices) or both.

Sudarshan Kriya Yoga (SKY) uses rapid breathing techniques to induce hyperventilation. Research at NIMHANS, Bengaluru, found SKY beneficial for depression; it is a low-risk, low-cost adjunct for stress, anxiety, PTSD, stress-related illnesses and substance abuse.

Meditation focuses attention on the breath or an object, thought or mantra. In vipassana (mindfulness-based) meditation there is no fixed object; the person passively observes bodily sensations and thoughts as they arise. Kundalini yoga, which combines breathing with chanting of mantras, has also been found useful for mental disorders.
Benefits include better mood, attention, mental focus, stress tolerance and overall well-being. People should learn these practices from trained teachers and continue medical care when needed.

example.q: Distinguish focused meditation from vipassana meditation.
steps: Focused meditation: attention is fixed on one object, such as the breath or a mantra.
Vipassana (mindfulness-based): no fixed object; one passively observes sensations and thoughts as they come and go.
example.answer: Focused meditation fixes attention on one object; vipassana observes everything passively without a fixed object.

learn.reallife: NIMHANS in Bengaluru has an integrated yoga programme, and many Indian hospitals now offer yoga as an add-on to standard treatment for depression and anxiety.

topics.title: Factors that heal and ethics in psychotherapy

learn.hook: Two clients get the same therapy; one improves fast, the other slowly. Healing depends on more than technique — and the therapist must follow strict ethics.
points: Factors contributing to healing: (1) the techniques used by the therapist; (2) the therapeutic alliance — the therapist's regular availability, warmth and empathy; (3) catharsis — emotional unburdening or release, often in early sessions.

(4) Non-specific factors: patient variables (motivation for change, expectation of improvement) and therapist variables (positive nature, absence of unresolved emotional conflicts, good mental health).

Ethics in psychotherapy: informed consent; confidentiality of the client; alleviating personal distress; integrity of the practitioner–client relationship; respect for human rights and dignity; professional competence and skills.
Informed consent means the client is told about the nature, purpose and possible effects of therapy and agrees voluntarily.

example.q: In her first session, Asha cries for a long time while describing her problems and later says she feels 'lighter'. Which healing factor is this?
steps: Emotional release while expressing problems.
This unburdening is catharsis.
example.answer: Catharsis.

learn.reallife: India's Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 gives people the right to confidentiality and to informed consent for treatment — the same ethical principles therapists follow.

topics.title: Rehabilitation of the mentally ill

learn.hook: Medicines may quieten the voices, but what about getting a job, making friends and planning a day? That's where rehabilitation comes in.
points: Treatment has two parts: reducing symptoms, and improving the person's level of functioning and quality of life. Rehabilitation aims to empower the patient to become a productive member of society to the greatest extent possible.
Many patients, especially with schizophrenia, have negative symptoms such as lack of interest and motivation; rehabilitation addresses these.

Occupational therapy: patients are taught skills such as candle-making, paper-bag making and weaving to help form a work discipline. Social skills training: interpersonal skills are developed through role play, imitation and instruction, so patients learn to function in social groups.
Cognitive retraining: improves basic cognitive functions such as attention, memory and executive functions.
Vocational training: once the patient has improved sufficiently, they gain skills needed for productive employment.

example.q: Plan rehabilitation for Raju, a young man recovering from schizophrenia who forgets instructions, avoids people and has never worked.
steps: Cognitive retraining for attention and memory problems.
Social skills training using role play to build interaction.
Occupational therapy (e.g. candle-making) to build work discipline.
Vocational training for a job once he is ready.
example.answer: Cognitive retraining, social skills training, occupational therapy, then vocational training.

learn.reallife: Centres like NIMHANS run day-care and vocational rehabilitation, and some Indian NGOs help recovering patients run small businesses such as tailoring units and cafés.

topics.title: Social psychology and the building blocks of social behaviour

learn.hook: Why do you clap louder when the whole stadium claps? Why do you trust some news channels and not others? Social psychology studies how others shape what we think, feel and do.
points: Social psychology is the branch of psychology that investigates how the behaviour of individuals is affected by others and by the social environment — how we think, feel and act in social situations.
In the rationalised CBSE syllabus, this chapter focuses on attitudes (their nature, formation and change, and the attitude–behaviour link) and on prejudice and discrimination.
Social behaviour is shaped by social cognition — the mental processes of gathering and interpreting information about the social world — and by social influence from others.
Attitudes, beliefs and values are the building blocks of social behaviour: they shape how we judge people, events and ideas, and how we act towards them.

example.q: Riya decides to stop using plastic bags after her friends start a 'no plastic' drive. Which aspects of social behaviour are involved?
steps: She gathers and interprets information about the drive — social cognition.
Her friends' behaviour affects her — social influence.
A new attitude towards plastic is forming — a building block of social behaviour.
example.answer: Social cognition, social influence and attitude formation.

learn.reallife: When neighbours in an Indian housing society all start segregating waste, newcomers quickly do the same — social psychology in action.

topics.title: Nature of attitudes and their A-B-C components

learn.hook: 'I love cricket' (feeling), 'I think cricket builds teamwork' (thought), 'I play every evening' (action). Three sentences, one attitude.
points: An attitude is a state of the mind — a set of views or thoughts regarding a topic (the attitude object) — that has an evaluative feature (positive, negative or neutral).

The tri-component (A-B-C) model: Affective component — the emotional part (feelings). Behavioural (conative) component — the tendency to act in a certain way. Cognitive component — the thought or belief part.
Attitude objects can be people, groups, objects, ideas or issues (e.g., attitude towards online classes, towards saving water).
Attitudes are fairly stable and help guide behaviour, though they can change.

example.q: Identify the A, B and C components: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution. I feel happy seeing green parks. I plant a sapling every monsoon.'
steps: 'I believe planting trees reduces pollution' → cognitive.
'I feel happy seeing green parks' → affective.
'I plant a sapling every monsoon' → behavioural (conative).
example.answer: Cognitive, affective and behavioural components respectively.

learn.reallife: The 'Swachh' cleanliness drives in many Indian cities try to work on all three components: information (cognitive), pride in a clean city (affective) and actual clean-ups (behavioural).

topics.title: Beliefs, values and features of attitudes

learn.hook: Rate your view on space exploration from 1 (very negative) to 5 (very positive). Your number reveals two features of your attitude: its valence and how extreme it is.
points: Beliefs are the cognitive component of attitudes and form the ground on which attitudes stand (for example, belief in democracy). Values are attitudes or beliefs that contain a 'should' or 'ought' aspect, such as moral values like honesty and hard work. Values form when a belief or attitude becomes an inseparable part of one's outlook on life, so they are hard to change.
Valence (positivity or negativity): on a 5-point scale (1 = very negative, 2 = negative, 3 = neutral, 4 = positive, 5 = very positive), a rating of 4 shows positive valence.
Extremeness: how positive or negative the attitude is. Ratings 1 and 5 are equally extreme and are more extreme than 2 and 4; a rating of 3 is the least extreme.

Simplicity or complexity (multiplexity): how many attitudes there are within a broader attitude. An attitude towards health and well-being, for example, includes many smaller attitudes (physical health, happiness, diet) — it is complex.
Centrality: the role of a particular attitude in the attitude system. A central attitude influences many other attitudes and is more resistant to change than peripheral ones.

example.q: Arjun rates his view of nuclear energy as 2, and Leena rates hers as 5 on a 1–5 scale. Compare valence and extremeness.
steps: Arjun: 2 → negative valence.
Leena: 5 → positive valence.
Extremeness: 5 is at the end of the scale; 2 is one step from neutral.
Leena's attitude is more extreme.
example.answer: Arjun's attitude is negative, Leena's is positive and more extreme.

learn.reallife: Survey agencies in India ask voters and consumers to rate views on 5-point scales — the numbers capture valence and extremeness of attitudes towards products and policies.

topics.title: How attitudes are formed

learn.hook: Why do you like a subject? Often it started with a teacher you liked. Attitudes are learned — and there are five main ways it happens.
points: Learning through association: a positive attitude towards one thing spreads to what it is linked with (e.g., liking a teacher leads to liking the subject she teaches).
Learning through rewards and punishment: being praised for a behaviour builds a positive attitude towards it (e.g., praised for doing yoga → positive attitude to yoga).
Learning through modelling (observation): watching others being praised or punished for holding an attitude or behaving in a certain way.

Learning through group or cultural norms: norms are unwritten rules about behaviour expected in a group or culture; over time they become part of our attitudes. Learning through exposure to information: books, the media and biographies of admired people shape attitudes.

Factors in attitude formation: family and school environment (especially in early years), reference groups (groups whose norms one accepts), personal experiences, and media-related influences (print, TV, internet — which can create both positive and negative attitudes).

example.q: Ishita sees her elder brother praised by the family for volunteering at a blood donation camp, and she develops a positive attitude towards volunteering. Which process is this?
steps: She did not volunteer herself or get rewarded directly.
She watched someone else being praised.
Learning by observing others = modelling.
example.answer: Learning through modelling (observation).

learn.reallife: Biographies of people like Dr A.P.J. Abdul Kalam have inspired positive attitudes towards science in many Indian students — an example of learning through exposure to information.

topics.title: Attitude change: Heider's balance and Festinger's dissonance

learn.hook: You know junk food is unhealthy, yet you eat it every day. That uneasy feeling? Festinger called it cognitive dissonance — and it pushes you to change something.
points: Heider's balance concept is expressed as a P-O-X triangle: P is the person whose attitude is studied, O is another person, and X is the attitude object. Each of the three relations (P–O, P–X, O–X) can be positive or negative.

Imbalance exists when all three sides are negative, or when two sides are positive and one is negative. Balance exists when all three are positive, or when two are negative and one is positive. (Tip: multiply the signs — a positive product means balance.)
Imbalance is uncomfortable, so the attitude changes in the direction of balance.

Festinger's cognitive dissonance: the cognitive components of an attitude must be consistent (consonant). If two cognitions are dissonant (e.g., 'Junk food harms health' and 'I eat junk food daily'), one of them is changed to restore consonance (e.g., 'I'll eat junk food only once a week').
Both balance and dissonance are examples of cognitive consistency: two components or elements of an attitude must be consistent with each other.

example.q: P (Priya) likes O (Omar), Priya likes cricket (X), but Omar dislikes cricket. Is this balanced? How might it change?
steps: P–O positive (+), P–X positive (+), O–X negative (−).
Two positive and one negative → product is negative → imbalance.
To restore balance, Priya may start liking cricket less, or persuade Omar to like it, or like Omar less.
example.answer: Imbalanced; one relation must change to restore balance.

learn.reallife: Anti-smoking ads in Indian cinemas create dissonance — 'Smoking kills' versus 'I smoke' — hoping viewers will resolve it by quitting.

topics.title: Mohsin's two-step concept and features of the existing attitude

learn.hook: Your favourite cricketer starts eating millets and posts about it. A month later, you're trying ragi dosa. An Indian psychologist explained this in two neat steps.
points: S.M. Mohsin's two-step concept: the target is the person whose attitude is to be changed; the source is the person through whose influence the change happens.

Step 1: the target identifies with the source — the target likes and regards the source highly and puts herself or himself in the source's place. The source should also have a positive attitude towards the target.

Step 2: the source actually shows an attitude change by changing her or his own behaviour towards the attitude object. Observing this, the target imitates the source and changes her or his attitude and behaviour.

Characteristics of the existing attitude affect change: attitudes in a state of imbalance or dissonance are more open to change; extreme and central attitudes are harder to change than less extreme or peripheral ones; simple attitudes are easier to change than complex (multiplex) ones.

Direction of change: congruent change (same direction — a positive attitude becomes more positive) or incongruent change (opposite direction — a positive attitude becomes negative). An extreme attitude is especially hard to change incongruently.

example.q: Neeraj admires his elder cousin, a doctor, who has always eaten fried snacks. The cousin starts eating fruits instead and talks about it. Neeraj soon does the same. Map this to Mohsin's steps.
steps: Target: Neeraj; source: his doctor cousin.
Step 1: Neeraj identifies with and admires the cousin, who is also fond of him.
Step 2: the cousin changes his own behaviour (eating fruits); Neeraj observes and imitates.
example.answer: Step 1: identification with the source; Step 2: source shows the change, target imitates.

learn.reallife: Public health campaigns in India often feature admired sportspersons who first adopt the behaviour themselves (e.g., getting vaccinated on camera), using Mohsin's second step.

topics.title: Source, message and target factors in attitude change

learn.hook: Why do toothpaste ads show a dentist in a white coat? Who says it, what is said and who hears it all decide whether attitudes change.
points: Source characteristics: credibility (a highly credible, expert source produces more change) and attractiveness (an attractive or likeable source produces more change).

Message characteristics: the amount of information (attitudes change most when the information is just enough — neither too much nor too little); rational appeal (facts, e.g. 'saves fuel') versus emotional appeal (feelings, e.g. 'loving families choose this'); the motives the message activates (such as health, safety or status); and the mode of spreading (face-to-face messages are more effective than indirect ones like letters or pamphlets).

Target characteristics: persuasibility (people with open, flexible personalities change more easily); strong prejudices make change less likely; low self-esteem people change more easily than high self-esteem people; more intelligent people may change less easily, though sometimes they change more willingly because they base attitudes on more information and thinking.
Analysing an advertisement: identify the source (who), the appeal (rational or emotional), the motive activated, and the intended target audience.

example.q: Analyse an ad: a famous cricketer smiles and says, 'Champions start their day with this cereal — be a champion!'
steps: Source: attractive and popular, not necessarily an expert in nutrition.
Appeal: emotional — wanting to feel like a champion.
Motive activated: achievement and status.
Target: young sports fans.
example.answer: Attractive source, emotional appeal, achievement/status motive, young sports-fan audience.

learn.reallife: Government health campaigns in India pair doctors (credibility) with film stars (attractiveness) and use both facts and emotions — covering all the bases of persuasion.

topics.title: Attitude–behaviour relationship

learn.hook: Almost everyone says littering is bad. Yet plastic bottles still pile up on beaches. Why don't our actions always match our attitudes?
points: Attitudes predict behaviour better when: the attitude is strong and occupies a central place in the attitude system; the person is aware of her or his attitude; there is very little or no external pressure to behave in a particular way.
Also when the person's behaviour is not being watched or evaluated by others, and when the person thinks the behaviour will have a positive consequence and so intends to engage in it.

LaPiere's study (1930s): LaPiere travelled across the USA with a Chinese couple and stayed in many hotels; they were refused service only once. Later, when hotel managers were sent a questionnaire asking whether they would accept Chinese guests, most said they would not — a gap between stated attitude and actual behaviour.

Behaviour can also shape attitudes. Festinger and Carlsmith asked students to do a very boring task and then tell others it was interesting. Students paid $1 for this later rated the task as more interesting than those paid $20 — with little external justification, they reduced dissonance by changing their attitude.

example.q: Why did the $1 students, not the $20 students, change their attitude towards the boring task?
steps: Both groups said the task was interesting, which conflicted with their experience.
$20 was enough external justification: 'I said it for the money.'
$1 was not enough justification, so dissonance remained.
They reduced it by believing the task really was interesting.
example.answer: Low payment gave too little justification, so they changed their attitude to reduce dissonance.

learn.reallife: Many Indians support saving water in surveys, but behaviour improves most when households can see their own usage and there are positive consequences, like lower bills — matching the conditions for attitude–behaviour consistency.

steps: In the later questionnaire, most managers said they would not accept Chinese guests.

Assertion (A): People may act differently from their attitudes when their behaviour is being watched by others.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

He will change his attitude to dislike saving power
quiz.explain: All the conditions for attitude–behaviour consistency are present.

topics.title: Prejudice, stereotypes, discrimination and their sources

learn.hook: 'People from that city are all rude.' One sentence — a stereotype, a prejudice and a possible seed of discrimination. Let's untangle them.
points: Prejudices are attitudes towards a particular group, usually negative and often based on stereotypes. A stereotype is a cluster of ideas about the characteristics of a group, assumed to be true of all its members; it is the cognitive component of prejudice and is often based on limited or incorrect information.
Discrimination is the behavioural component — negative actions towards members of a group. Prejudice can exist without discrimination, and discrimination can occur without prejudice.
Sources: learning — prejudices are learned through association, rewards and punishment, observation, group norms, family, reference groups, personal experiences and the media.

A strong social identity with an ingroup and ingroup bias can lead to negative attitudes towards outgroups. Scapegoating: a majority group blames a weaker minority outgroup for its own social, economic or political problems.

Kernel of truth: stereotypes may persist because there may be a small element of truth in them. Self-fulfilling prophecy: the target group behaves in ways that confirm the prejudice (e.g., a group labelled 'dull' loses motivation and performs poorly), keeping the prejudice alive.

example.q: Label each: (a) 'All engineers are boring' (thought), (b) feeling dislike for engineers (feeling), (c) refusing to rent a flat to engineers (action).
steps: (a) A generalised belief about a group = stereotype (cognitive).
(b) A negative feeling/attitude towards the group = prejudice.
(c) Negative action = discrimination (behavioural).
example.answer: (a) Stereotype, (b) Prejudice, (c) Discrimination.

learn.reallife: The Indian Constitution prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15) — law tackles discriminatory behaviour, while education targets prejudiced attitudes.

quiz.mistake: Thinks they always go together.

quiz.q: A group labelled 'lazy' loses motivation and performs poorly, which seems to confirm the label. This is:
quiz.explain: The target's behaviour confirms the prejudice.
steps: The group labelled 'lazy' behaves in a way that confirms the label.
That is a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Answer: Self-fulfilling prophecy
quiz.mistake: Thinks the label must have been true.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Strong identification with one's own group can increase prejudice towards outgroups.
Reason (R): Ingroup bias leads people to view outgroups more favourably than their own group.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: ingroup bias means favouring one's own group and viewing outgroups less favourably.
steps: A: strong ingroup identity can increase prejudice towards outgroups – true.
R: ingroup bias makes outgroups look more favourable – false; it favours one's own group.
So A is true, but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of ingroup bias.

quiz.q: The 'kernel of truth' concept suggests that:

quiz.explain: A small grain of truth can keep a stereotype alive, even though it is overgeneralised.

Answer: Stereotypes may persist because they contain a small element of truth
quiz.mistake: Treats the 'kernel' as proof the stereotype is right.

teach.praise: Chirp! Thinking is a stereotype, disliking is prejudice, chasing away is discrimination. I'll be fair to crows!

topics.title: Strategies for handling prejudice

learn.hook: Put students from rival schools on one team for a national science fair. By the end, the 'rivals' are friends. Contact under the right conditions can melt prejudice.
points: Strategies are effective if they aim at: minimising opportunities for learning prejudices; changing negative attitudes; de-emphasising narrow social identity based on the ingroup; and discouraging the tendency towards self-fulfilling prophecy among victims of prejudice.
Education and information dissemination: correcting stereotypes about specific target groups and tackling strong ingroup bias.

Increasing intergroup contact (the contact hypothesis): direct communication removes mistrust and helps groups discover positive qualities in each other. It works best when the groups meet in a cooperative rather than competitive context, interact closely, and are not different in power or status.
Working towards shared, superordinate goals that neither group can achieve alone encourages cooperation and reduces ingroup–outgroup hostility.
Highlighting individual identity rather than group identity weakens the importance of group membership as a basis for judging others.

example.q: A college finds tension between students from two hostels. Suggest two strategies based on psychology.
steps: Create mixed teams for a project both hostels need to complete (cooperative contact with a superordinate goal).
Run information sessions correcting stereotypes each hostel holds about the other.
Encourage students to know each other as individuals, not just as 'Hostel A' or 'Hostel B'.
example.answer: Cooperative intergroup contact with shared goals, education to correct stereotypes, and emphasising individual identity.

learn.reallife: India's school exchange programmes — students from different states living with host families — use the contact hypothesis to build understanding across regions and languages.

quiz.q:

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Both are true; when these conditions are missing, contact can even increase hostility.

R: it works mainly in cooperative, close, equal-status contact – true.
Without those conditions contact can fail.
So both are true and R correctly explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks any contact automatically reduces prejudice.

topics.title: What is a group? Features, and how groups differ from crowds, teams and audiences

learn.hook: Forty people waiting at a bus stop and eleven players in the Indian cricket team — both are 'people together'. But only one is a true group. What's the difference?
points: Groups influence how we think and act. (In the rationalised syllabus this chapter covers the nature and formation of groups, types of groups, and group influences such as social loafing and group polarisation.)

A group is an organised system of two or more individuals who interact and are interdependent, have common motives, have set role relationships among members, and have norms that regulate members' behaviour.

Features: a social unit of two or more people who see themselves as belonging to the group; common motives and goals; interdependence (one member's actions affect others); members trying to satisfy needs through joint association and influencing each other; interaction governed by a set of norms; and defined roles.

A crowd is a collection of people present at a place by chance, with no structure, no feeling of belongingness and no interdependence; crowd behaviour can be irrational. An audience is a collection of people gathered for a special purpose, such as a film or a cricket match; it is generally passive, but may sometimes turn into a mob.

A team is a special kind of group whose members have complementary skills and are committed to a common goal, for which they hold themselves mutually accountable. In groups, performance depends on individual contributions; in teams, both individual contributions and teamwork matter, producing positive synergy.

example.q: Classify: (a) people gathered after a minor road accident, (b) a school's quiz team with a history expert, a science expert and a sports expert, (c) viewers at a cinema hall.
steps: (a) Gathered by chance, no structure → crowd.
(b) Complementary skills, common goal, mutual accountability → team.
(c) Gathered for a special purpose, mostly passive → audience.
example.answer: (a) Crowd, (b) Team, (c) Audience.

learn.reallife: An ISRO mission team brings together engineers with complementary skills — propulsion, software, navigation — all accountable for one launch. That's a team, not just a group.

topics.title: Why people join groups and how groups form

learn.hook: Why do you join a WhatsApp group of classmates, a dance club or a coaching batch? Each one fills a need — and some are formed simply because you sit close together.
points: Security: being in a group reduces insecurity and gives comfort and protection. Status: membership of a recognised group gives a feeling of importance, power and status.
Self-esteem: groups give feelings of self-worth and a positive social identity. Satisfaction of psychological and social needs: belongingness, giving and receiving attention, love and power.
Goal achievement: groups help achieve goals that cannot be achieved alone. Knowledge and information: groups provide information and widen our knowledge.

Group formation factors: proximity (repeated interaction with people nearby, such as classmates or neighbours), similarity (people like those with similar interests and attitudes; similarity also validates our views) and common motives and goals.

example.q: Ananya joins her college's robotics club because (a) she wants to build a robot for a national contest, (b) club members are known as the 'tech elite' on campus, and (c) she can learn from seniors. Name the reasons.
steps: (a) Achieving a goal not possible alone → goal achievement.
(b) Being part of a recognised, admired group → status.
(c) Learning from others → knowledge and information.
example.answer: (a) Goal achievement, (b) Status, (c) Knowledge and information.

learn.reallife: Hostel friendships in Indian colleges often start simply because students live on the same floor — proximity at work.

topics.title: Stages of group formation and group structure

learn.hook: A new project team: first awkward introductions, then arguments over who does what, then a rhythm sets in — and finally they deliver. Tuckman mapped this journey.
points: Bruce Tuckman's stages: Forming — uncertainty about the group, its goal and how to achieve it; members get to know each other; excitement and apprehension. Storming — intragroup conflict over how to achieve the goal, who controls the group and resources, and who does which task; at the end, a hierarchy of leadership develops.

Norming — members develop norms about group behaviour, leading to a positive group identity. Performing — the group's structure has evolved and is accepted, and the group works towards its goal (the final stage for some groups).

Adjourning — once the purpose is achieved, the group may be disbanded (e.g., a committee formed for a school function). Groups do not always move through the stages in a fixed order; they may go back and forth.

Group structure develops as members interact: roles (socially defined expectations people are expected to fulfil), norms (expected standards of behaviour and beliefs, agreed and enforced by members — the group's unwritten rules), status (the relative social position given to members; it may be ascribed, as through seniority, or achieved, through expertise or hard work) and cohesiveness (togetherness and mutual attraction among members — the 'we-feeling').

example.q: Map a school annual-day committee to Tuckman's stages: (1) members meet and feel unsure, (2) they argue over who will host, (3) they agree on rules for rehearsals, (4) they put on the show, (5) the committee is dissolved.
steps: (1) Forming
(2) Storming
(3) Norming
(4) Performing
(5) Adjourning
example.answer: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning.

learn.reallife: IPL franchise squads assembled through auctions go through forming and storming in pre-season camps; the best ones reach norming and performing quickly.

topics.title: Types of groups

learn.hook: Your family, your school's NCC unit, your lunch-break gang and the rival school's team. Each is a different type of group — and each affects you differently.
points: Primary groups are pre-existing formations usually given to the individual (such as the family). They involve face-to-face interaction, close physical proximity and warm emotional bonds, are central to individual functioning, shape values and ideals, and have less permeable boundaries.

Secondary groups are joined by choice (such as a professional association or a hobby club). Relationships are more impersonal, indirect and less frequent, and it is easy to leave and join another group.

Formal groups have explicitly stated functions, roles and rules (such as an office, a university or a school council). Informal groups form without specific rules, and members have close relationships (such as a group of friends).

Ingroup refers to one's own group ('we'); outgroup refers to another group ('they'). Ingroup members are seen as similar and are viewed favourably; outgroup members are often seen differently and less favourably.

Other collectivities include crowds (chance gatherings), audiences (gathered for a purpose, generally passive) and mobs (with a definite sense of purpose, polarised attention, homogeneity of thought and behaviour, and impulsivity).

example.q: Classify the group types: (a) Rohit's family, (b) the Bar Council he joins as a lawyer, (c) his group of college friends, (d) his company's HR department.
steps: (a) Given, warm, face-to-face → primary (and informal).
(b) Joined by choice, impersonal → secondary (and formal).
(c) No set rules, close bonds → informal.
(d) Explicit rules and roles → formal.
example.answer: (a) Primary, (b) Secondary/formal, (c) Informal, (d) Formal.

learn.reallife: When two IPL franchises clash, fans strongly feel 'us' versus 'them' — a vivid example of ingroup and outgroup feelings, which is healthiest when the rivalry stays friendly and respectful.

topics.title: Social facilitation and social loafing

learn.hook: In tug-of-war, does each extra person pull as hard as they would alone? Experiments say no — and the reason has a name: social loafing.
points: Social facilitation: performance on well-learned or simple tasks improves in the presence of others (Norman Triplett found cyclists rode faster when racing with others than alone). The presence of others raises arousal; for new or complex tasks, performance may instead suffer.

Social loafing is a reduction in individual effort when working on a collective task, in which outputs are pooled with those of other members (e.g., tug-of-war). Latané and colleagues found people clapped and cheered less loudly per person in groups than alone.

Reasons: members feel less responsible for the overall task; motivation decreases because individual contributions are not evaluated; the group's performance is not compared with other groups; there is improper or no coordination; and belonging to the group is not important to members — it is only an aggregate of individuals. (Responsibility is spread or diffused across members.)

Reducing social loafing: make each person's effort identifiable; increase pressure to work hard by making members committed to successful performance; increase the apparent importance or value of the task; make people feel their individual contribution is important; and strengthen group cohesiveness.

example.q: In a group project, only Riya does most of the work while others contribute little. Suggest two ways the teacher can reduce social loafing.
steps: Assign each member a specific, named part so individual effort is identifiable.
Make the project important (e.g., a public presentation) and build cohesiveness so members care about the outcome.
example.answer: Make individual efforts identifiable and increase task importance and group cohesiveness.

learn.reallife: In big office meetings in Indian companies, people often stay quiet expecting 'someone else will speak up'. Assigning named action points reduces that loafing.

topics.title: Group polarisation and groupthink

learn.hook: Each member of a committee mildly favours a new flyover. After an hour of discussion, the group votes to build it immediately, whatever the cost. How did 'mild' become 'extreme'?
points: Group polarisation: groups are more likely to take extreme decisions than individuals alone; the group's initial position becomes stronger after discussion.

Reasons: (1) in the company of like-minded people, members hear new arguments favouring their own viewpoint; (2) when others share the same view, members feel their view is validated by the public — a bandwagon effect; (3) members perceive like-minded others as an ingroup, identify with the group and conform, so views become strengthened.

Groupthink (Irving Janis) is a related, extreme outcome of highly cohesive groups: the desire for consensus overrides realistic evaluation of alternatives. Signs include an illusion of unanimity, self-censorship of doubts and pressure on dissenters, often leading to poor decisions.
Preventing poor group decisions: encourage critical evaluation, invite outside opinions, and assign someone to play 'devil's advocate'.

example.q: Before discussion, each member of a school council mildly supports banning phones on campus. After discussion they vote for a total ban with heavy fines. Explain using the reasons for group polarisation.
steps: Members heard new arguments supporting the ban (more reasons to agree).
Seeing others agree validated their view (bandwagon effect).
Identifying with the like-minded group led them to conform and strengthen the position.
example.answer: Exposure to new supporting arguments, bandwagon validation and ingroup identification made the decision more extreme.

learn.reallife: Social media echo chambers in India and elsewhere show group polarisation online: like-minded users share supporting posts, and views grow more extreme over time.
